activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles.
story:
The stadium smelled like burnt ketchup and cold air, and Sebastian found his seat between his grandfather and Marylou just as the national anthem ended. Maxwell was two rows down with his father, wearing a jersey so new the folds still creased the numbers. It was the third quarter of Sebastian's life, in a way, the last game he would attend before he left for college in the fall, and he had promised himself he would pay attention to everything.

His grandfather had been quiet through the coin toss, which was unusual. Then, during a punt, the old man leaned over and said, "You know I saw the first one of these. The very first Super Bowl."

Marylou turned around from her popcorn. "No way."

"Green Bay Packers against the Kansas City Chiefs. I was there." He said it the way he said most things, flat and certain, like a man reading a courtroom verdict.

Sebastian did the arithmetic without meaning to. His grandfather was seventy-nine now, which meant he had been eleven in 1967. Eleven, and living in Dayton, Ohio, in a house Sebastian had visited every Christmas of his childhood. He did not say anything yet. The teams lined up, the stadium made its slow seismic noise, the kind that started in the concrete and climbed through the soles of your shoes, and a running back broke free for thirty yards and the crowd swallowed itself.

At halftime he took out his phone and looked it up, partly to settle the question and partly because Marylou had been trying to contextualize the whole afternoon for him all week, telling him this game was a threshold, an ending, a door, and he wanted something harder than metaphor to hold onto. The record said the first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles. He read it twice. The score his grandfather remembered. The teams. But the stadium had been in Los Angeles, on the fifteenth of January, and his grandfather had been an eleven-year-old in Ohio.

He sat with that for a while, watching the marching band spell out letters he couldn't read from the upper deck. Marylou nudged him. "What's the face for?"

"He wasn't there," Sebastian said quietly. "He was a kid in Ohio. It was in Los Angeles."

"So he's lying?"

"I don't think so." And he didn't. He thought about how his grandfather told stories, how the old man never lied but sometimes moved himself inside them, the way he'd claimed for years to have shaken a governor's hand when really he'd stood in a crowd the governor had waved at. It wasn't lying. It was circumlocution, almost, a long way around a smaller true thing, and Sebastian had spent enough summers on that porch to know the difference mattered.

Meanwhile Maxwell had a crisis of his own going, three rows down. He had put twenty dollars into the squares pool at his father's office, and the final digits on his square were five and zero, and for three quarters the score had refused him, drifting from 7 to 3 to 17 to 13, so close and then not. His father kept telling him to stop checking his phone, and Maxwell kept checking anyway, holding the screen low like a man hiding cards.

In the fourth quarter Sebastian leaned toward his grandfather. "The first one was in Los Angeles, right? In January."

"January fifteenth." The old man didn't look away from the field. "My brother's friend had a television, the only one on the street with any color in it, and we all crowded into that room. Thirty-five to ten." He was quiet a moment, then added, "I suppose I say I was there because it felt like being there. Nobody had ever seen anything like it."

Sebastian nodded. It was the most honest version of the story he was going to get, and somehow it was better than the first version, an eleven-year-old boy in Dayton watching a thing happen in Los Angeles that nobody had ever seen before. He could not prove the television part, and he decided he didn't want to. Some things you filed under probably true and left alone.

Down in the end zone the home team scored, and the scoreboard flickered, and Maxwell stood up with both hands on his head because the score now ended in five and zero. His father pulled him into a hug that lifted him half off the ground, and Marylou laughed and grabbed Sebastian's sleeve, and his grandfather was still watching the field with the small, satisfied look of a man keeping score in his head against everyone else's.

"Next year," the old man said, "you'll be watching from some dormitory."

"Probably on a laptop the size of a postcard," Sebastian said.

"Packers by twenty-five," his grandfather said. "You heard it here first."

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: The Haggadah is the book read aloud at a Passover Seder; it retells the story of the Israelites' exodus from slavery in Egypt.
story:
The cemetery gate was still open, though the light had begun to fail, and Olivier walked the gravel path to the third row of stones without needing to think about the turns. His grandfather had been in the ground for five months. In the car, his mother had said they would only stay a minute, and then had stayed eleven, wiping the granite with the heel of her hand as though it were a kitchen counter. Now she was back at the car with his father, and Olivier was the one who remained, holding the battered paperback his grandfather had left him in the drawer of the desk nobody else was allowed to open.

The book was a Haggadah. "It's the book we read aloud at the Seder," his grandfather had told him one April, tapping the cover with two fingers, wine-stained and duct-taped at the spine. "It retells the story of the Israelites' exodus from slavery in Egypt. Whole thing, start to finish, every year." Olivier had been eleven then and had mostly cared about the matzah ball soup. But this year his grandfather would not be at the head of the table, and someone had to sit in his chair, and his grandmother had looked at Olivier across the shiva candles and said, "You know the order, bubbeleh. You've heard it your whole life."

That was the problem. He had heard it his whole life, which was not the same as knowing it. Last night, at Miley's kitchen table, he had spread the Haggadah out between two mugs of tea and tried to divide it into parts. His cousin Miley, seventeen like him and allergic to ceremonies in general, leaned over his shoulder. "Why are you cutting it up like a ransom note?"

"Because Grandpa never just read it himself," Olivier said. "He handed out pages. Everyone got a turn. Aunt Ruth with her terrible Hebrew, Uncle David doing the plagues in funny voices." He moved a photocopied page across the table. "If I just read it all myself, it's a lecture. If I hand it out wrong, people stumble and it gets embarrassing and everyone just wants dinner."

"So make it simple."

"Simple isn't the point." He heard how that sounded, like an aphorism his grandfather might have coined after the fourth cup of wine, and he softened it. "I don't know what the point is. But it's not simple."

He remembered, then, a Seder from when he was nine. It had gone interminably, or so it had felt at the time, his stomach growling while the reading stretched past nine o'clock, and he had whispered to his grandfather, "Can we skip to the food?" His grandfather had not scolded him. He had leaned close, smelling of wine and pepper, and said, "The story is the food, Olivier. The rest is just soup." At nine, Olivier had thought this was a dodge. Now, at the stone, in the cold, he wondered whether his grandfather had been telling him something about what a family actually does when it gathers, which is feed itself a story it already knows, on purpose, the way you water a plant you can see.

The wind moved through the cemetery and he put the book inside his jacket. That was when he noticed he was not alone. Mr. Kang, from two doors down, the neighbor who had helped carry the shiva chairs, was standing a few rows over with a small rake, clearing leaves from a grave Olivier didn't recognize. Mr. Kang caught his eye and raised a hand.

"You're the grandson," Mr. Kang said, coming nearer. "The one who's taking over the dinner."

"Trying to."

"My wife did everything for our holidays," Mr. Kang said. "Chuseok. The food, the order, who bows first. When she passed, I thought, I'll just buy the food, that's the hard part." He turned the rake over in his hands. "The food was the easy part. I could have sued somebody for the rest of it. Nobody can indemnify you for a thing like that, you understand? No amount of money puts it back." He laughed, short and dry, at his own joke, and Olivier laughed too, because there was nothing else to do with it.

"Did you figure it out?" Olivier asked.

"I did the whole thing badly for three years," Mr. Kang said. "My daughters corrected me. Now it's mine, badly, with their corrections. That's the version we have." He looked at Olivier, at the shape of the book under his jacket. "You'll do your grandfather's badly, and then it will be yours."

In the car afterward, his mother asked if he was all right, and he said yes, which was mostly true. At home he laid the torn pages out on the dining room table, around the good dishes, one at each seat, and where the pages didn't reach, he wrote names on napkins. Aunt Ruth would get the passage with the repetitive refrain, because she liked having something to hold on to. Uncle David got the plagues, obviously. Miley, who hated Hebrew, got the shortest English section, and he wrote beside her name, "You have to do the frogs voice." For his grandmother he left the Four Questions to give to the youngest kid, because that was the chair she had always leaned on his grandfather to remember.

He kept the last page for himself, the one that ended with next year in Jerusalem, which his grandfather had always read alone, slowly, looking at each face around the table in turn. Olivier read it once aloud to the empty room to feel the weight of it in his mouth. Then he set his grandfather's Haggadah on his grandfather's chair and went to check on the soup.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: SQL was developed at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, and was first called SEQUEL.
story:
The bell for last period had already rung, and Mr. Gupta's deadline stood where it always stood: queries submitted to the shared folder by 3:15, no exceptions, no amnesty for anyone who spent the period arguing instead of typing. Zoe had twenty-two minutes and a blank file.

The lab smelled like warm plastic and the lemon cleaner the janitor used on Fridays. Kassandra leaned across the aisle, tapping Zoe's screen where the prompt sat waiting. "It's pronounced sequel. Everyone says sequel. My cousin works at a bank and she says it all day."

"S Q L," Joy said from the next row, not looking up. "It's an acronym. You don't say scuzz-ball for S-Q-L, you spell it out."

"You literally just said scuzz-ball."

Zoe muted them both, in her head if not in the room. Her assignment read: write a query that lists every customer who has never placed an order. She understood the two tables, customers and orders, each sitting there like guest lists for two different parties. What she could not see was how to find the people who were on one list and absent from the other. Absence was the whole point. Databases were terrible at absence; they recorded what happened, and what never happened left no row, no field, no tidy cell.

She typed an inner join first, the join Mr. Gupta had demonstrated on Tuesday, and the result came back as a wall of names, every one of them a customer who had ordered something. Exactly backwards. She deleted it and tried a subquery, nesting one SELECT inside another the way a diagram in her notes showed, and the database answered with a red error that debilitated her more than its length justified: syntax near line 4. She had been sure of line 4.

"It was originally called SEQUEL," Kassandra was saying behind her. "So that settles it."

"That's not evidence, that's a rumor," Joy said. "Look it up if you're so confident."

Zoe, who was already in a browser tab because procrastination and research look identical for the first four seconds, typed the rumor in herself before Kassandra could. The result came back faster than her error had. SQL was developed at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, and it was first called SEQUEL. She read it twice, then turned around in her chair.

"It's real," she said. "IBM, early seventies, two guys named Chamberlin and Boyce. It was first called SEQUEL."

"So I'm right," Kassandra said.

"So you're right about history," Joy said, "and wrong about now. Things change. Names change."

The clock gave Zoe eighteen minutes. She looked at the two tabs side by side, the argument and the manual, and something about the history nudged her. If the language had been renamed once, it could hold more than one way of asking. She went back to her query and typed LEFT JOIN, then sat staring at it. Left join. Keep every row from the left table, the customers, whether or not anything matched on the right. Then, in the WHERE clause, she asked for the rows where the order's ID was NULL, which felt like asking a question about nothing. She ran it.

Three rows. Three customers, real names from the seed data, who had never ordered anything. The database had found absence by looking sideways at it.

At 3:11, before she could submit, Mr. Gupta's reply arrived to the message she had sent that morning asking for an extension. She opened it while Joy read over her shoulder. "No extension," the message said. "But if your first attempt fails, submit anyway. Failed queries earn feedback, and feedback is worth more than silence. You have until 3:15 like everyone else. Also, settle the pronunciation argument yourselves; I refuse to be parochial about it."

"That's not even what parochial means," Joy said.

"It's close enough."

Zoe copied her query into the submission folder at 3:14, one minute inside the deadline, and felt the small, private satisfaction of a thing built rather than guessed. Kassandra turned around in her seat, vindicated, still quoting IBM. "Chamberlin and Boyce, Joy. The seventies."

"Fine," Joy said. "You get the past." She pointed at the screen, where the submission confirmation had just refreshed. "But look at your results."

The first row of the three customers who had never ordered anything was the account Zoe herself had created two weeks ago to test the system, her own name sitting in the customer table, having ordered nothing.

"Congratulations," Joy said. "You queried yourself."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review, so its findings have not yet been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal.
story:
Olivier had promised Ms. Friedman the review by Monday, and by Sunday afternoon he still didn't have a position, only two articles and a headache. So he took the bus to his grandfather's house, where the kitchen table was enormous and nobody asked him to explain himself before noon. His grandfather met him at the door in a cardigan with a burn hole near the pocket, which Olivier chose not to mention, since the last time he had mentioned it he'd been assigned a lecture on the merit of wool.

The two articles both asked whether city trees measurably lower summer temperatures in poor neighborhoods, which sounded like a simple question until Olivier read them. The first had been published in a journal with a long name and a lot of commas; the second had appeared only on a website his grandfather's desktop could barely load, a plain page with the article title in big gray letters and a banner across the top that read PREPRINT. Not published. Not rejected, either, which was somehow worse, because rejection at least was an answer.

He spread both papers across the table and weighted the corners with saucers, because the back door was open and the wind off the garden was capricious, slamming the screen one minute and going dead the next. His grandfather set down a mug of tea and studied the arrangement like a man inspecting a chessboard mid-game. "Two of them and one of you," he said. "That's usually called a problem, but sometimes it's called an education."

While Olivier read, his phone buzzed. It was Keagan, who was apparently spending his Sunday the same way, except with more complaining.

Tried the library thing Friedman said about finding TWO sources. Found one from a journal and one that's just on some website?? It says PREPRINT at the top. Did you get that too? Is the website lying? Did I do the assignment wrong? Also is your grandpa's house the one with the plum tree because I need plums, my mom is making something.

Olivier typed back that yes, there was a plum tree, and no, Keagan hadn't done it wrong, and then stopped, because he realized he didn't actually know what a preprint was. He'd assumed it was like a rough draft, unfinished, but the article looked complete, charts and everything. He opened the banner page and read the small print beneath it twice. The paper had been posted publicly before peer review, which meant, as far as he could tell, that its findings had not yet been checked by the independent experts a journal would choose. Nobody had lied to Keagan. Nobody had verified anything, either.

"So which one wins?" his grandfather asked, sliding into the opposite chair. "The journal one, obviously, yes?"

"It's not obvious," Olivier said. "The journal one is three years old and only covers two cities. The preprint covers eleven, and it's from this spring. But nobody's checked it."

"Then you have a current liar and an outdated honest man."

"That's not what I said."

"No," his grandfather agreed, buttering toast he'd apparently been carrying the whole time. "But it's funnier when I say it." He chewed for a while, stoic about the crust, which was burned. Olivier watched him not complain about it and thought about how his grandfather had spent forty years as a machinist, a job where a measurement was either right or the part didn't fit, and how he still liked questions that came apart the same way. This one didn't. The preprint wasn't wrong and wasn't right; it was unjudged, and Olivier had to judge it anyway, on the record, with his name at the top.

He started drafting right there at the table, and the drafting was slower than the reading had been. He wrote that the journal article deserved more weight because it had survived review, then deleted it, because that made it sound like survival was the only thing that mattered, and the eleven cities kept nagging at him. He wrote that the preprint offered newer and broader data, then deleted that too, because "newer and broader" was exactly the kind of phrase a person uses to preempt a question he can't actually answer. Finally he wrote it straight: the two articles could be read together, the older verified one as a floor and the newer unchecked one as a ceiling of what might be true, and he could not yet say whether the truth sat nearer the floor or the ceiling. He sat back. It felt unsatisfying, like leaving a door open on purpose.

His phone buzzed again. Keagan had found a preprint of his own for his project on sleep and grades and was asking, in three texts of increasing panic, whether citing it would "count." Olivier typed: It counts as a preprint. Posted publicly before peer review, so nobody's checked it yet. Say that in your paper and use it carefully. Then he added, Plums are on the tree behind the garage, take the low ones, the crows get the rest.

"Did you solve it?" his grandfather asked, collecting the saucers.

"Sort of. I figured out how to be honest about what I don't know."

"Hmph," said his grandfather, which in his language meant approval. He paused at the counter. "Your grandmother used to say that about cooking. Follow the recipe you trust, but taste the thing that isn't in the book yet."

Olivier looked at his draft, at the sentence about floors and ceilings, and realized he wanted to keep it. He saved the file, folded the two articles into his bag, and went out to hold the ladder while Keagan, arriving on a bicycle with a backpack already half full of somebody else's plums, called down from the branches, "Take the low ones, he says. The low ones are all gone, man. Everything down here is basically a rock."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Kintsugi is a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold, treating the break as part of the object's history rather than hiding it.
story:
The bowl broke on the Tuesday Tyson stayed to clean his grandmother's kitchen while she was at physical therapy, because she had asked him to, twice, and because the second ask had been quieter than the first. He was only moving the drying rack to wipe beneath it. The bowl had been balanced on top of the plates, and when it hit the tile it split into four pieces with a sound like a knuckle cracking, and Tyson stood very still for a while, holding a dish towel, listening to the house tick.

He gathered the pieces before she came home. He set them on his desk upstairs, in the room that had been his father's, fitting them together like a puzzle to prove to himself it could be done. His grandmother had said the bowl was from her mother, which meant it had crossed an ocean and two divorces and forty years of moves, and he could not stand the thought of telling her he had ended it in a rented kitchen with a dish towel.

At school the next morning he told Elina in the parking lot, hands jammed in his jacket pockets. "I can glue it back," he said. "Superglue. She'd never look that close."

"She looks at that bowl every day," Elina said. "You told me that yourself. It's on the windowsill." She was quiet for a second, then less quiet. "There's this thing Nia told me about once. From Japan. Kintsugi. You repair broken pottery with lacquer, and you mix the lacquer with gold, or dust gold powder over it, so the crack shows on purpose."

Tyson frowned at the hood of a car that wasn't his. "Gold where the break is."

"Right. The idea is the break is part of the thing's story. You don't hide it." Elina shrugged, already half-turned toward the doors. "Nia knows more than me. Ask her in Pritchard's class."

Ms. Pritchard's fifth period was art, which Tyson had taken because he needed the credit and because Elina had promised to sit next to him. He asked Nia while Ms. Pritchard wrote something about form on the board. Nia pulled out her phone, showed him photographs: bowls and cups veined with seams of gold, glowing like frozen lightning. "Real lacquer, urushi, takes forever to cure," she said. "Nobody here has that. But there's gold mica you can mix into slow-set epoxy. It's not the real thing. It's the idea of it."

"The idea of it," Tyson repeated. He was trying to decide whether an imitation of a tradition was a betrayal or a tribute, whether you could dichotomize it so cleanly at all. "That feels like the difference between honoring something and copying it."

"It feels like that to me too," Nia said. "Do it anyway."

He worked on it at the kitchen table for three evenings, which was a risk, since the whole point was that his grandmother not see. The epoxy was thick and glistening, more ductile than he expected, and he learned quickly that gold powder hides nothing; it announces. Where he had imagined delicate veins, he got crooked bright ridges, each one a record of how steady or unsteady his hand had been that minute. He did not try to perfect them. He was starting to understand that was the wrong instinct.

On the third evening he heard the cane on the linoleum and did not hide the pieces fast enough. His grandmother lowered herself into the chair across from him and looked at the bowl, which was nearly whole again, its fractures drawn through with gold like rivers on a map. "That's Mother's bowl," she said. Not a question.

"I broke it," Tyson said. "Tuesday. I was going to glue it so you wouldn't know." He turned it so she could see the largest seam. "This is kintsugi. Sort of. Nia says it's the idea of it. The gold makes the break part of the story instead of pretending it never happened." He stopped there, because the rest of what he thought, about how the teleology of a thing might include its accidents, how a bowl broken and mended holds more time than a whole one, was not a sentence he could say out loud to her.

His grandmother picked it up and tilted it toward the window. Her thumb moved along the gold, slow, the way she touched the banister going upstairs, testing the world for steadiness. "It's louder than it was," she said. "Before, nobody looked at it twice." She set it down in the middle of the table instead of returning it to the windowsill, where it had sat unnoticed for years, and turned it once more so the light caught every seam. "Leave it here."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the second line of the staff, marking that line as the G above middle C.
story:
Grandmother's piano had gone flat in the years since anyone tuned it, and Gavin told Zain it didn't matter, which was mostly true and partly the kind of thing he said so he wouldn't have to admit he couldn't tell the difference yet. The assignment from Mr. Novák was due Thursday: sixteen bars, a melody with chord changes, written in standard notation, no exceptions. Zain had finished his in one evening, some looping thing built from a video game theme, and had driven Gavin out here because, as he put it, "You need a piano and no Wi-Fi, and your grandma has both."

She had also made lemonade, which was really sugar with citrus ambitions, and she sat in the kitchen doorway with her crossword while Gavin sat on the piano bench with Zain's half-empty manuscript paper beside him. His first attempt at writing the melody down had come out wrong. He'd played a phrase he liked, four bars that finally sounded like something, and when he notated it and played it back from the page, everything sat a step away from where he'd meant it. He played the phrase again, then the page again, then pressed both hands flat on the keys.

"It's doing the thing," he said. "Where it's right but it's wrong."

"That's called you," Zain said, not looking up from his phone.

Gavin leaned over the manuscript. He had copied the clef the way he always copied it, quickly, from memory, a curl he'd drawn on homework since middle school without ever thinking about what it was. But his grandmother, who had sung in choirs for fifty years, had shown him her old songbooks yesterday, and in the neat printed staves of one of them he noticed the curl did not float the way he drew it. It wrapped around a line. Specifically the second line of the staff, the one that sat second from the bottom. He drew it his way again and stared, then drew a small note on that second line.

"Zain. The treble clef is the G clef. The curl circles the second line. That line is the G above middle C." He tapped the page. "Mine circles the space above it. So everything I wrote shifted."

"So everything you wrote is garbage, is what you're telling me."

"No, it's just in the wrong place. It's the same melody sitting wrong."

They fixed it together, or rather Gavin fixed it while Zain held the lemonade and offered commentary, and once the notes landed where his hands had put them, the melody came back whole. Better than whole. In the second phrase he heard something he hadn't intended, a lean toward a minor chord he hadn't planned, and he sat with it for a long moment before writing A minor above the bar and letting the third phrase answer it. His grandmother looked up from the crossword and said, "That one. Play that one again," and he did, and she closed her eyes, and Gavin thought about how his mother kept saying the old place made Grandma sad, pathologizing every quiet afternoon she spent here as if solitude were a symptom needing a diagnosis rather than a preference. He wasn't sure. He was seventeen and there was no affidavit he could file about what his grandmother felt, only the fact that she asked him to play the phrase again.

By dusk he had eight bars he trusted and eight he didn't. Zain had left an hour before, and the creek behind the property had gone turbid with the rain that came through around six, the water brown and quick where it had been clear that morning, and Gavin stood at the window watching it while his hands remembered the phrase. He thought about Zain's loop, finished in a night, and about the printed songbooks in the front room, decades of other people's melodies written out in ink by hands that had known exactly where the curl went. He had drawn that clef wrong for years without anything breaking, because nothing had depended on it. Now something did.

He went back to the bench and worked the ninth bar until it stopped fighting him. It was nearly dark when his grandmother came in and turned on the small lamp, and she said the piano had been her mother's, and that nobody had played it since the funeral, and Gavin played the eight bars again with the wrong ones after them, because she hadn't asked for only the good part.

"Keep going," she said.

"It's not done."

"Neither am I," she said, and set the crossword down on the closed lid, pencil still in it, three squares blank.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 2 hypertension means a systolic reading of 140 or higher or a diastolic reading of 90 or higher.
story:
The printed case study had been staring up from Emma's binder all through lunch: 142 over 88, recorded at a clinic visit, with a note in the margin in her own handwriting, "bottom number fine??" Her grandmother's actual reading, three weeks ago, had looked exactly like that, and the nurse had said something that stuck in Emma's throat ever since. Tomorrow Emma had to stand up in health class and explain a blood pressure reading to her peers, and she could not make the two facts sit together.

She dragged Maelle into the second-floor bathroom before fifth period, because the bathroom had the long mirror and the radiator that made it warmer than the library, and because Maelle was the only person Emma knew who would rehearse anything without laughing. Cassius came too, on the grounds that the hallway was boring, and leaned against the sink with the case study held at arm's length like it might smear.

"Okay," Emma said, flattening the paper on the counter between two faucets. "I'm the presenter. You're the class. 142 over 88. The top number is systolic, when the heart pushes; the bottom is diastolic, when it rests. My grandma got that exact reading. And the nurse called it stage 2 hypertension, and I didn't say anything because I was too busy panicking."

Cassius turned the paper sideways, as though orientation were the problem. "But eighty-eight is under ninety," he said. "That's the good one, right? Lowish."

"That's what I thought." Emma had thought it all the way home on the bus, and then again at midnight. She flipped to the page she'd photographed from the course pack, the one she'd read four times without it ever quite landing. Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 2 hypertension meant systolic 140 or higher, or diastolic 90 or higher. She said it out loud, slowly, tapping the counter twice on the word "or." "It's not both. Either one does it."

Maelle, who was braiding and unbraiding a strand of her own hair, stopped mid-loop. "So her top number, 142, that's already over the line."

"By two points," Emma said. The whole thing suddenly seemed smaller and larger at once. Two points, and a word with a weight to it. She had looked up the etymology the night before, the way she did when a word frightened her, breaking "hypertension" into its Greek parts until it stopped sounding like a verdict and started sounding like a description. She told them that, and Maelle nodded like it was reasonable, and Cassius said words were just words, and Emma said that was exactly the point, that a word could be a door instead of a wall.

"So tomorrow," Maelle said, turning Emma by the shoulders toward the mirror, "say it to yourself. Pretend the mirror is the class."

Emma did, and it was terrible. She eulogized her draft as she went, burying sentence after sentence mid-delivery, but the part that mattered kept surviving. Diet and exercise could bring numbers down, she said; salt mattered, and so did moving most days, and her grandmother had already started walking with the neighbor's dog before work, dragging herself out into the diurnal routine she'd claimed to despise, complaining the whole way and then, lately, not complaining. What Emma could not promise, and would not, was how far down the numbers would go, or how fast, or whether her grandmother would keep walking when winter came. She said that part too, into the mirror, because it felt dishonest to leave it out.

Cassius, who had been quiet for a while, said his uncle had a cuff in a drawer somewhere and a piece of paper from a doctor he'd never understood. He asked whether the "or" worked the other way, a low top number with a high bottom one, and Emma said she thought so but she'd check before she claimed it, and he said fair, and Maelle said the bell was in two minutes.

They stood there a moment longer, the three of them reflected in the fluorescent light, the paper damp at one corner where the faucet had dripped. Emma folded it along the crease she'd made and made herself say the whole fact once more, cleanly, without the tap on the counter. Then Maelle snapped her binder shut and said, "That time it sounded like you," and Emma picked up her bag.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
The video arrived in the group chat at 9:14 on a Tuesday night, and by morning half the school had seen it. It showed floodwater roaring through a parking garage, brown and fast, with a caption in bold letters claiming it was the garage under the Riverside mall, filmed that afternoon. Nevaeh had sent it to Avery with six exclamation points and the message "WE HAVE TO WARN EVERYONE." Avery had watched it four times, and each time a small cold doubt tapped her on the shoulder, the way her grandmother used to tap her when she was reaching for a third helping of cake.

At lunch, Iman was already drafting a post. "If it's real, we should share it before the mall floods again," he said, thumbing through screenshots. "If it's real," Avery said, and Nevaeh rolled her eyes so far back she claimed she could see her own thoughts. "It has, like, forty thousand views," Nevaeh said. "So did the guy who claimed he was a virtuoso violinist and it turned out he was air-guitaring to a recording," Avery said. Iman snorted rice onto the table.

Here was the thing Avery hadn't told them yet. Last month, waiting out a dentist appointment at her mother's office, she had drifted to the desk of her mother's colleague, a patient man with two monitors, and watched him drag a video into a small toolbar and click. Frames had bloomed across his screen like a contact sheet. He'd caught her staring and let her try it, which was how she'd spent a corporate Tuesday afternoon in a swivel chair, feeling faintly like a spy. She said, "Library after school. Bring the video. Trust me for twenty minutes."

The library smelled like radiator dust and old glue, which Nevaeh declared romantic and Iman declared evidence that the heating system predated the internet. Ms. Ivanova, at the front desk, raised an eyebrow at their mission statement. "Verification," Avery said. "We're being responsible citizens." "Responsible citizens return books on time," Ms. Ivanova said, stamping something with unnecessary force, and pointed them toward the computers by the window.

Avery installed the plugin while narrating in what she hoped was a professional voice. "It's called InVID-WeVerify," she said. "It came out of a European Union-funded project." "Which you know because," Nevaeh prompted, arms crossed in cheerful skepticism. "Because a man with a lanyard showed me, and I was bored, and I remember things when I'm bored. It's my gift." Iman leaned in. "Okay but what does it do."

Instead of answering, Avery pasted in the video's link and clicked. The toolbar went to work, and the flood split apart, not into motion anymore but into still frames, a row of key frames lifted out of the video like cards fanned across a table. "Oh, that's clever," Iman said, before he could stop himself sounding impressed. Each frame carried a little button underneath. "Now it reverse-searches these," Avery said. "The images, not the video. The images go look for their older selves."

The oldest selves were easy to find. The very first frame, the one with the crooked parking sign, had been photographed three years earlier during flooding in a country none of them had ever searched for anything about. Nevaeh scrolled the results with her mouth slightly open. "So forty thousand people are sharing a parking garage on another continent." "With better parking signs than ours," Iman said. "Honestly it's a downgrade for the flood." Nevaeh threw a rolled-up receipt at him.

She was quiet for a second, typing and deleting a message, and Avery let her be quiet, because she knew the feeling: not the sting of being wrong exactly, but the stranger sting of realizing how badly you'd wanted it to be shareable. "I think the video works because it's affective," Avery offered. "It gets you in the body before it gets you in the brain. And after enough of them you get desensitized anyway, so you have to share fast, before you stop caring." "That's the most hopeless thing you've ever said in a library," Nevaeh said, and then, grudgingly, "Okay, show me the button thing. I want to check one about the chemistry teacher and a stolen golf cart."

Avery pulled up the plugin again, spun the chair toward Nevaeh, and slid the keyboard across. "Paste the link," she said. "Frames first, then feelings."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A pyramid with a wide base and narrow top shows a high birth rate and a young population, pointing to a growing need for schools and teachers.
story:
The minivan smelled like sunscreen and the apricots Gurnoor's mother had packed in a paper bag that was now leaking. They were four hours out of the city, driving south to the border, on their way to look at a school a volunteer organization wanted to rebuild, and Jack was in the back seat with his laptop balanced on his knees because the battery only held a charge if it lay perfectly flat.

"You're going to be a gourmand of data by the end of this," Gurnoor said, twisting around from the front. "You've eaten three hours of statistics."

"One of us has to know what we're walking into," Jack said. The organization had sent them two profiles. One was the country they were actually visiting; the other was a wealthier one where the same group ran eldercare programs. Ms. Nolan, who had arranged the trip before twisting her ankle and staying home, had emailed them a single instruction: figure out which one needs more classrooms, and be ready to say why on Monday.

The laptop slid. Jack caught it, and the page on his screen tilted with it, a population pyramid for the country they were driving toward. He had seen the shape before, in March, in a classroom he was now remembering without wanting to. Ms. Nolan had put a blank grid on the board and told them to guess where the people were, and Harlow, who had guessed nothing all year, had raised her hand and said, "It looks like a Christmas tree that fell over." The class laughed, and Ms. Nolan hadn't corrected anyone. She had just drawn, in green marker, bars that spread wide at the bottom and thinned toward the top, and said, "A pyramid with a wide base and narrow top shows a high birth rate and a young population, pointing to a growing need for schools and teachers." Then she'd capped the marker and moved on to the reading, and Jack had copied the sentence into his notebook because it was one of the few things all year that sounded like it was about something.

In the van, he opened the second profile. This pyramid was almost the opposite shape, narrow at the bottom, heavy in the middle and upper bars, like a barrel standing on its head. He sat with both pages side by side and felt something assemble itself, slowly, the way a seatbelt buckle finds its click.

"So which one gets the school," Harlow said from the driver's seat. She had claimed driving rights on the grounds that she was the only one who could change lanes without flinching.

"Ours does. The one we're visiting." He turned the laptop so Gurnoor could see. "Look. Wide base, narrow top. Tons of young people, high birth rate. That means schools, classrooms, teachers. The other one, that shape, they're going to need the eldercare thing more than classrooms." He heard himself say it and checked it against Ms. Nolan's sentence in his memory, and it held.

"Explain it again but slower," Gurnoor said, "and while you do that, hand me an apricot, because I've become a gourmand of those too."

Jack passed the bag and explained it slower, tracing the bars with his finger, and for the first time all summer he had the feeling of two separate things joining: the sentence he'd copied in March and the actual road under the actual tires, the actual town ahead where somebody was supposedly going to break ground on a second classroom. He was honest with himself about the gap, though. A shape on a page told you a population was young. It didn't tell you whether the town wanted the school, or whether the organization's money would arrive, or whether the teacher they'd promised would stay past the first hard season. The pyramid said the need pointed one way. What people did about it was a different subject, the one Ms. Nolan always said had no graphs.

They crossed the border at noon and the traffic slowed to something torpid, a line of trucks idling in heat that came through the windows like a hand pressing on the back of Jack's neck. Harlow drove with her wrists draped over the wheel. Gurnoor fell asleep against the window and woke up with a red line on his forehead, which he discovered in the visor mirror and pronounced, with dignity, "a second eyebrow."

The school, when they reached it in the late afternoon, was one long concrete building with a corrugated roof and a yard of packed dirt where forty or fifty kids were playing something that involved a ball and a great deal of shouting. A man who introduced himself as the school's only teacher came out to meet them, wiping his hands on a rag. He asked if they were the group from the north. Jack said yes, then, because there seemed no reason not to, said he'd looked at the numbers, at the shape of the population, and expected there were a lot of children here.

"More every year," the teacher said. He looked at the yard the way you look at weather coming in. "I have fifty-one in my class this term. Next year, more."

Jack took out his notebook, the same one from March, and wrote 51. It wasn't a graph. It was better than a graph, and it wasn't enough either, and both of those things were true at once. The kids in the yard had stopped playing and were staring at the van with the frank curiosity of people who had decided the visitors were the most interesting event of the week. One small girl came close to the fence, cupped her hands around her mouth, and shouted something in a language Jack didn't know.

"She wants to know if you brought a ball," the teacher said.

"We didn't," Jack said. "We brought apricots."

The girl's face went through several rapid calculations, and then the whole yard, as one body, started running toward the fence.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
story:
Ella had counted the money twice before she ever earned any of it. The guitar in the window of the shop on Marsh Street cost four hundred and ten dollars, and her mother had said, in the careful voice that meant no, that lessons were one thing and wanting was another. So when the coffee shop near the school put a sign in its window, Ella went in with a folded resume that listed the bake sale she'd run in tenth grade and the babysitting she'd done for the neighbors, and the manager, a tired man with a laminated schedule taped to his forearm, hired her on the spot. Two weeks of training, he said. Then she'd be on her own with the register.

Emilee came in on Ella's first real shift and ordered a hot chocolate she didn't want, just to watch Ella work. "You look official," she said, leaning on the counter while the milk steamed. "You look like a person who knows where the lids are."

"I know where three kinds of lids are," Ella said. "There's a fourth kind. I've heard rumors."

The rumor about the fourth kind of lid turned out to be true, which Ella took as a good omen. She learned the register, the mop that jammed if you pushed it wrong, the regulars and their orders. Mr. Balogun, who lived two doors down from her and came in every morning for a large black coffee, started greeting her by name. He was retired from something he never specified, and he read the newspaper at the window table for exactly forty minutes each day. When she mentioned the job to him, he nodded and said, "Hourly, I hope, and non-exempt." She didn't know what the second word meant, but she wrote it on her wrist anyway, in ballpoint, because Mr. Balogun tended to say things that mattered later.

Winter break arrived, and with it a small crisis: two of the other employees had the flu, and the manager asked Ella whether she could cover their shifts. She said yes before she'd done the arithmetic. Then she did the arithmetic. Between her regular hours and the extra shifts, she was down for fifty-one hours that week, and she spent a nervous evening assembling an inchoate plan to fake her way through the exhaustion, suture it together with coffee and willpower, and still be pleasant to customers at seven in the morning on the fifth consecutive day. Murray, who had taken the bus with her since seventh grade, listened to all of this and said only, "You're going to smell like espresso forever. That's your recompense."

The first week broke her in ways she hadn't predicted. Her feet ached in a new place, behind the ankles. She mixed up Mr. Balogun's coffee once and he drank it anyway, which felt worse than if he'd complained. On the last double shift, she and Murray sat in the back room with their coats on, splitting a day-old croissant, and she said, "I don't even know what I'm getting paid for this. Probably the same as always. Probably they just expect it."

Then the paycheck came, and it did not look the way she expected. She had done the math on her phone, lying on her bedroom floor: eleven hours, ten dollars an hour, one hundred and ten dollars. The stub showed her regular rate for most of her hours, and then, further down, a different line, a higher rate, applied to eleven of them. She counted the hours in the week, all fifty-one of them, and counted them again. The higher rate had kicked in for every hour past forty.

She took the stub to the window table the next morning, laying it beside Mr. Balogun's coffee like evidence. "Does this look right to you?"

He put on the glasses he kept folded in his shirt pocket and studied it. "It's the law," he said. "Hours past forty in a workweek, one and a half times your regular rate. That's what non-exempt means." He tapped the line with one finger. "You worked more than forty, so those hours paid extra. They didn't do you a favor. They did what they had to."

Ella sat with that for a moment, the small strange warmth of it. She had imagined the extra shifts as a favor she was doing them, a debt she was quietly absorbing, and it turned out the accounting ran in both directions. It wasn't generosity. It was a rule with a number in it, and the number had worked for her without her knowing. She thought of her mother's careful voice, of the guitar in the window, and recalculated: at this rate, three more heavy weeks, maybe two.

She was still smiling at the arithmetic when the manager came over with the new schedule in his hand. He set it on the counter and slid it toward her.

"Flu's over," he said. "You're at forty exactly this week."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Orthodox or traditionalist historians of the Cold War, writing mainly in the late 1940s and 1950s, blamed its outbreak chiefly on Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe.
story:
Mya spread her notebook across the library table so that both books faced her at once, like witnesses in the same trial who refused to agree. On her left, a thick volume with a cracked spine argued that the United States had overreacted after the war, manufacturing a threat where there had mostly been exhaustion. On her right, a slimmer book, older, its paper gone the color of weak tea, took the opposite view. She had forty minutes before the library closed and a paper due Friday, and so far her notes consisted of one sentence with a question mark after it.

"What's the question mark for?" Misha asked, sliding into the chair across from her with a bag of sunflower seeds he was not supposed to open indoors.

"That's the whole problem," Mya said. "The question mark is the paper."

Misha looked at the two books, then at her, then at the clock, phlegmatic about everything as usual, as if deadlines were weather that happened to other people. He had come to the library to copy a chemistry lab he'd left at home, and he settled in to watch her work the way people watch a tennis match they don't follow.

The old book was the one that bothered her. She had found it shelved wrong, in the travel section between a guide to Norway and a pamphlet about fjord cruises, and she'd carried it to the front desk to ask if it could be reshelved. Mr. Aquino, the librarian, had looked at it, looked at her, and slid it across the counter instead of taking it.

"That's a famous one," he said. "First edition. The orthodox school."

"The what?"

"Orthodox historians, writing mainly in the late 1940s and 1950s, blamed the outbreak of the Cold War chiefly on Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe." He said it the way he said the fire exit was past the copier. "That's the traditional view. You'll want the revisionists too if you're being fair." And he'd pointed her toward the thicker book without asking what she was doing, which she appreciated.

So now she had both, and the problem was that both of them cited evidence. That was the part nobody had warned her about. She had assumed disagreements between historians were like disagreements between her parents, where one side was exaggerating and you just had to figure out which. But the old book quoted Soviet actions in Eastern Europe, one after another, with dates she copied down, and the newer book quoted American decisions, also with dates, also real. Neither seemed to be lying. She wrote "both cite evidence?" and then crossed out the question mark and wrote "both cite evidence," because a question mark was not an argument.

Charity arrived at twenty past, breathless, having run from swim practice, and dropped into the third chair. "Tell me you're done and we can get food."

"I'm emancipating myself from my own paper," Mya said. "It's going to be free and I'm going to be free of it."

"That's not what that word is for, but okay." Charity stole a sunflower seed. "What's it on?"

"The Cold War. Who started it. I have one book saying it was basically the Soviets, and one saying the Americans turned it into a war so they'd have something to be against. And I have to pick."

"So pick the one with the better evidence."

Mya looked at the table, at her two columns of notes, at the dates that did not match up neatly because events never happened in the order that made essays easy. "They both have evidence. The old one was written closest to when it happened, but that's also when everyone was scared and angry. The new one had fifty years of archives, but by then the argument itself was fifty years old. It's like the time the information comes out shapes what the information is." Charity blinked at her. "I think," Mya added, "I think that's what I'm going to write."

"You're going to write that you don't know?"

"No. I'm going to write that the traditional view blames the Soviet Union, that the revisionist view blames the United States, that both have evidence, and that where they can't both be right, the evidence I have can't settle it. And then I'm going to say why that's not the same as having no opinion." She pulled a fresh page toward her and started writing fast, before the sentence could fall apart.

Mr. Aquino passed with a cart of returns and slowed beside their table. "Closing in ten minutes," he said, and then, seeing the old book open under her hand, "You can take that one out. It's been sitting in the wrong section for a decade. At least it's being read."

"You put it in the travel section on purpose, didn't you," Mya said.

Mr. Aquino pushed the cart on without answering, and Misha cracked another sunflower seed with his teeth and said, "Ten bucks says the fjord books moved themselves."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Near the edges of real plates the field lines bulge outward and the field weakens, an effect called fringing, so E = V/d holds best near the centre.
story:
Morgan had taped the graph to the corner of her trifold at seven that morning, and by ten she still could not stop looking at it, because the graph was wrong. Not wrong in the way of a smudged axis or a flipped sign; wrong in the way that meant she was missing something. She had built two aluminum plates, fifteen centimeters apart, wired to a high-voltage supply borrowed from the physics lab, and she had computed the field strength between them the way the textbook said: divide the voltage by the distance. Twelve thousand volts across fifteen centimeters gave eighty kilovolts per meter, clean and uniform, a number you could set your watch by. Then she had suspended a small charged foil sphere between the plates on a thread and measured the force on it at different positions, and everywhere near the middle the number came back beautifully close. Near the edges, it collapsed.

"You're going to wear a groove in the table," Kohl said from the next booth, where his own project, a wind turbine made of printer parts, was drawing a small crowd of third graders. He leaned over the tape line dividing their territory. "Every judge that stops, you point at the graph like it insulted your family."

"It did insult my family," Morgan said. "I checked the voltage four times. I recalibrated the foil charge. It's not me."

Kohl picked up one of the third graders' dropped juice pouch and handed it back before the kid could cry about it, then came around to her side of the tape. He studied the graph upside down, which was apparently how he did his best thinking. "So the field is weaker out here," he said, tapping the drooping tail of her data. "Near the edge of the plates."

"By a lot. Like a third."

"Is your thing broken, or is physics broken?"

That was the question, and she didn't have an answer, and the first judges were circulating already in their lanyards and clipboards, pausing at Raphaelle's booth across the aisle, where Raphaelle was explaining her model of river meanders with more confidence than Morgan had ever mustered about anything. Raphaelle caught her eye over the judges' heads and mouthed, you okay? Morgan mouthed back, no idea, and Raphaelle held up one finger: one minute, and she'd come over. That was Raphaelle. She had finished her own presentation early specifically so she'd have time to help other people with theirs, and she'd once told Morgan that she planned to monetize the skill eventually, tutoring rates, but for now it was free.

When the first judge arrived at Morgan's booth, a retired engineer with reading glasses on a chain, Morgan walked him through the setup, the derivation, the predicted value, and then, because hiding the graph would be worse than showing it, she showed him the graph. "My measurements near the center agree with the prediction," she said. "Near the edges they don't. The field there is weaker than the formula gives."

The judge nodded slowly and wrote something on his clipboard, and she could not tell if it was a good something or a bad something. "And what do you conclude?" he asked.

She had prepared three conclusions on the drive over. The first was that her apparatus was flawed, which the repeated measurements argued against. The second was that the formula itself was wrong, which felt presumptuous, like telling a river it had meandered incorrectly. The third, the one she had been circling all morning without landing on, was that the formula was an idealization, true under conditions the textbook hadn't bothered to spell out. "I think," she said, "the equation assumes something about the plates that stops being true at the edges." The judge's pen paused, then moved again, and he said, "Interesting," in a tone that gave away nothing, and moved on to Kohl's turbine.

Raphaelle appeared two minutes later, still holding one of her river diagrams like a shield. "Okay, tell me everything," she said, and Morgan told her everything, the numbers, the voltage checks, the foil sphere, the drooping tail of the graph, and while she talked she realized she was talking herself somewhere. The equation divided voltage by distance and said nothing about position, so it was claiming the field was the same everywhere between the plates. Her data said otherwise only near the edges. So whatever the equation assumed, it was an assumption about the middle, about being far from an edge, about the plates being, in effect, infinite, the way the blank white page of a proof is infinite even though the paper in your hand is not. Real plates ended. Of course the physics knew they ended. Of course the middle was where the lie was smallest.

"Here," Raphaelle said, pulling out her phone. "Search your own name plus the word, I saw it when I was looking up your project last night for my own, don't be flattered. It's called fringing." She turned the screen around. Morgan read the paragraph twice, and it was all there, stated plainly, the way facts you've already deduced always look when you finally find them written down: near the edges of real plates the field lines bulged outward and the field weakened. The equation held best near the center. Her graph hadn't been broken. It had been a map of exactly where the textbook's promise ran out.

"There it is," Morgan said. "Fringing."

"Say it louder, the second judge is circling."

Ms. Aydın was the second judge, which was either fortune or its opposite, since she was the physics teacher who had signed out the voltage supply to Morgan in the first place with the warning, delivered over her glasses, not to touch anything without the grounding strap. She stood in front of the trifold with her hands clasped and let Morgan go through the whole thing without interruption, the derivation, the measurements, the discrepancy, and then the word, offered up like something Morgan had dug out of the ground herself. "Near the edges, the field lines bulge outward and the field weakens," she said. "It's called fringing. So the formula, the voltage divided by the distance, holds best near the center, and my data shows that. The disagreement isn't an error. It's where the ideal case ends."

Ms. Aydın looked at the graph for a long moment, then at the plates, then back. "And what would you measure," she said, "if you made the plates larger and kept the gap the same?"

Morgan saw it before she finished hearing the question: more center, less edge, a smaller and smaller territory where the ideal gave way. "The agreement would hold over a bigger region," she said. "The fringing wouldn't go away. It would just matter less."

Behind her, Kohl's turbine had stopped turning and the third graders were losing interest, and Raphaelle was already crossing the aisle to spin one of the blades and point at the little LED lighting up, saying, watch this part, this is the good part.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US National Labor Relations Act does not cover government employees, agricultural workers, domestic workers, supervisors or independent contractors.
story:
The warehouse stood at the edge of a cabbage farm outside town, and Nicolas got the job the week school ended, through a cousin of a cousin who said the packing shed always needed hands in July. He was hired on the spot, told to bring work gloves, and handed a form that called him an independent contractor. He signed it without reading the small type because he needed the money for tuition deposits, and because he was seventeen and assumed the paper was routine.

His cousin Eugenie worked at a distribution warehouse in the city, the kind with loading docks and forklifts, and when she visited that first weekend she described her job the way other people described citizenship. She had a contract, seniority, a break schedule someone had fought for, and a union rep named only as the rep, as if there could be no other. "We bargain together," she said. "One voice, three hundred people. Management has to sit down with us." Nicolas said it sounded good, and he meant it, and he thought about his own paper form the whole drive home.

On Monday he asked the shift supervisor, Mr. Morin, whether the shed had a union. Mr. Morin was sorting turnips into crates and did not look up. "No union here," he said. "We're covered under the farm." Nicolas asked what that meant. "It means what it means." A man stacking pallets nearby laughed once, not unkindly, and went back to stacking.

Nicolas worked ten hours that day, then eleven on Wednesday, and when Friday's envelope came the pay was straight time all the way through. At Eugenie's warehouse, he knew, anything past eight was time and a half, written into the contract. He counted the envelope twice, then counted what he'd expected, and the difference was the price of his textbooks for one class.

He found the answer himself, at the public library, on a Saturday when his hands had recovered enough to hold a pen. The National Labor Relations Act, the book said, did not cover government employees, agricultural workers, domestic workers, supervisors, or independent contractors. He read the list twice. He was two of the five, possibly three, depending on how a court would adjudicate the question of what he actually was, since the form said contractor and the work said farm laborer. Either way, the law's door was closed. He photocopied the page, which felt like an action, and put it in his glove compartment, where it stayed.

That week a woman on the line, older than the rest, cut her hand on a crate strap and was told to bandage it and keep sorting, which she did. Nicolas watched her wrap the strap differently afterward, padding it with cardboard, teaching the person beside her the trick without stopping her rhythm. Nobody filed a complaint. He understood, watching, that there was no procedure to file one into, no form that would reach anyone, and that his own sense that this was an indictment of the whole arrangement was a private thought with no office to receive it.

He tried anyway, in the small ways available. He asked Mr. Morin, at the end of shift, whether overtime could be paid at a higher rate even without a requirement, and Mr. Morin said the farm's margins were thin and that Nicolas was free to renegotiate his own rate, alone, like any contractor. "That's the deal you signed," he said. So Nicolas renegotiated. He asked for a dollar more an hour, alone in the office with the door open, and he got forty cents, and he understood the forty cents as what one voice was worth in a room of one.

Eugenie came out again in August, and they sat on the tailgate of her car eating peaches from a roadside stand. He told her about the list in the library book. "So farm workers, domestic workers, government employees, supervisors, contractors," she said, counting them off on sticky fingers. "None of us. That's most of the people I know, actually." She said it without drama. Nicolas said he'd gotten forty cents, and she laughed and said the rep would have gotten him a dollar and a grievance process, and also that the rep would never take his call, because he wasn't in the bargaining unit, because there was no bargaining unit.

School started in September and Nicolas left the shed,Envelope-less now, with savings that were smaller than planned and larger than nothing. He kept the photocopy. When Daniel, his roommate, asked why a page about labor law was taped inside his desk drawer, Nicolas said, "Read the list," and went to find his shower shoes, and Daniel stood there reading it.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Peak bone mass is typically reached in the early twenties in women and the late twenties in men, so bone built in the teenage years affects bone strength for life.
story:
The kettle had just begun to murmur when Isla found her grandmother in the chair by the window, left leg propped on a cushion, the hospital bracelet still on her wrist like a souvenir she hadn't decided whether to keep. Isla had taken the bus straight from school, her trainers still in her bag, because the coach had said Thursday's session was optional and Amy had texted that they could abscond to the cafe near the river instead, just this once, just for the whole of exam season. She had almost said yes. She was still holding the unsent reply when she let herself in with the key under the geranium pot.

"Sit," her grandmother said. "You can pour." There was a pamphlet on the side table, the hospital's crest on the cover, and beside it a photograph that had not been there before: a young woman on a trail above a treeline, squinting into bright montane air, a rucksack riding high on her shoulders. It took Isla a moment to recognize the jawline, the particular set of the mouth. "You broke it on a hill," she said. "That's what Mum told me."

Her grandmother laughed, then touched her hip as though reminding it to behave. "A hill, technically. I tripped on a scree slope I had no business crossing at my age, and I have been informed by three separate professionals that I was very lucky." She held out her cup. "The surgeon said the bone itself is in remarkable condition. Whatever I was doing at your age, apparently it held."

Isla poured the tea slowly, watching the steam. On the pamphlet's back page, in the corner, a line of small print she had glanced past on her way to the kitchen caught her again now: it mentioned the age at which bone mass peaks, early twenties in women, and she turned the page over as if checking whether the sentence would still be there. It was. She looked up at her grandmother, at the propped leg, at the photograph of the squinting girl. "And it doesn't come after that? For anyone?"

"For men it comes later," her grandmother said. "The late twenties, the doctor told me, when I asked. Then it's whatever you've got." She sipped her tea. "Whatever you built before, that's the account you draw on."

That evening, after her grandmother had gone up to bed with her crutch clicking a slow rhythm on the stairs, I sat in the window chair with my bag at my feet and the pamphlet open on my knee. Amy's text was still unanswered. I understood, in a way that felt less like being told something and more like finding a room in a house I had lived in for years, that Thursday's optional session was not really about Thursday. It was about an account being filled or not filled, deposit by deposit, in a decade I was in the middle of and could not feel. I had been running a quiet dialectic in my head for weeks: the present self who wanted the cafe, the river, the long unstructured afternoons before everything narrowed into exams, and some future self I couldn't picture, some woman of sixty or eighty who would either trip on a hill and get up, or not. Both selves were mine. Only one of them was doing the choosing.

The twist came when I went to hang the pamphlet back on its table and found, tucked beneath it, a folded sheet of the hospital's headed paper, in my grandmother's handwriting, dated that morning. It was a list. Signed up for the physiotherapy follow-up. Phoned the rambling club about summer. Asked about the gentle walks at the reservoir. And at the bottom, circled twice: asked whether great-granddaughters can come along, or granddaughters, or anyone at all who is seventeen and thinks she is too busy.

I stood there a long moment with the paper in my hand. She had known I might come. She had left the photograph out for me to find, and the pamphlet, and this. It was not quite the same as being told what to do; it was closer to being handed evidence and left alone with it, which was, I was beginning to see, her way of loving people. She had built her bones on trails before anyone had told her why, and then at eighty-two she had crossed a scree slope she shouldn't have, and broken, and healed, and signed up for more. The deposits had not saved her from falling. They had, as far as I could tell, saved her from something worse, though I couldn't have named exactly what, and I didn't try.

I took out my phone. To Amy I wrote, cafe Friday instead, and then, before I could argue with myself, I opened the message from the coach, the one about the optional session, and tapped going. Then I carried my trainers up to the guest room and set them by the door where I would see them first thing, laces loose, ready.

From the landing below came my grandmother's voice, mild and half asleep through the wall: "Isla, is that you still down there?"

"It's me," I called back. "Go back to sleep. I'm just putting my shoes by the door."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: A launch velocity v at an angle θ above the horizontal splits into a horizontal component v cos θ and a vertical component v sin θ.
story:
The playground behind the elementary school had one of those old rocket slides, painted orange, and Raphael had chosen it as his study spot because no one under ten was there at six in the evening. He spread his physics worksheet on a bench, weighted the corners with his phone and his keys, and read the problem again. A ball launched at twenty meters per second at thirty degrees above the horizontal: how far does it go. His father had said college would expect him to figure things out on his own now, and had said it the way you hand someone a heavier bag to carry.

Jake arrived with a basketball under his arm and Jewel trailing behind him with a slushie, and both of them dropped onto the swings as if the bench, the worksheet, and Raphael's whole ambition were decorative. "You're doing homework at a playground," Jewel said. "That's the saddest thing I've seen all week." Raphael said it was quieter than his house, which was true, and also that Ms. Lin had told him the test was curved, which was also true, though she'd said it with a look that suggested the curve would not rescue anyone who couldn't decompose a vector.

"Watch," Raphael said, because he needed an audience and they were the only ones available. He took the basketball from Jake and rolled it along the bench, flat and fast. "If I launch it at almost zero degrees, like basically flat, it should just go sideways, right? Zoom, skimming." He wanted to check the math against the world. He found the angle in his notes, thirty degrees, and wrote the horizontal component as twenty sine thirty, and the vertical as twenty cosine thirty, because sine and cosine looked alike at eleven at night and at six in the evening too. He multiplied and got ten for the horizontal push and about seventeen for the upward push, which meant the ball would spend most of its energy climbing. He stared at the numbers, then at the flat-rolling basketball, then at the numbers again.

"According to this," he said slowly, "a ball launched almost flat would fly almost straight up." Jake laughed, the easy laugh of someone with nothing at stake, and Jewel stopped her swing with her heel. "Then the math's wrong," she said, "or the ball is wrong." Raphael felt the particular humiliation of holding two true-seeming things that contradicted each other, and also the smaller, sharper feeling underneath it, that the error was his, that he had swapped the two functions and built a rocket out of a ground ball.

He texted Ms. Lin, half expecting no answer, but she replied within a minute with a single line: "Horizontal is v cos theta, vertical is v sin theta." He read it aloud. At thirty degrees, cosine gave about seventeen for the sideways component and sine gave ten for the vertical, and now the numbers agreed with the bench and the rolling ball and, he suspected, with the entire visible universe. He tried the edge cases the way she'd taught them to test an answer: ninety degrees, straight up, and the horizontal component went to zero, all the velocity pouring upward; zero degrees, and the vertical component vanished, everything running flat. The geometry held together the way a good sentence does, every clause supporting the others.

He stood on the bench, which Jewel told him was an abrogation of playground law, and held the basketball at thirty degrees from horizontal, or what he hoped was thirty degrees, arm cocked, eyeballing the slide as a target. "If I throw at twenty meters per second," he said, "most of it goes sideways, about seventeen, and only ten goes up, and the ten going up is what gravity drags down while the seventeen just keeps going." He threw. The ball clipped the edge of the slide, banked off the monkey bars, and landed in the woodchips a full meter from where his new calculation predicted. "A meter off," Jake said. "Your physics is a meter off." Raphael said the meter was in his arm, not in the math, and believed it about eighty percent, which was more than he'd believed anything all week.

They took turns throwing after that, calling out angles like they were calling audibles, and Jewel kept score of whose landing came closest to the prediction, and it occurred to Raphael that he had turned his friends into auxiliary measuring instruments without their consent. There was a small bathos in it, he thought, the grand laws of motion being verified by three teenagers and a borrowed ball in a schoolyard, the whole majestic architecture of physics descending to woodchips and a dented basketball. He didn't mind. The descent felt like company.

When the light went amber and Jewel claimed the last slushie sip and Jake spun the ball on one finger, all exhibition, Raphael copied the clean version of the problem into his notebook. He still didn't know why sine took the vertical and cosine the horizontal, only that they did, and that the world voted with them. That gap sat in him like a tooth he kept testing with his tongue. He zipped his bag, pocketed his keys, and before they left he threw the ball once more, flat and hard, low over the woodchips, and watched it skim the ground almost the whole way to the fence.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1982 Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as German chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence, the only time the procedure has succeeded at the federal level.
story:
Tyson spread the two index cards on the kitchen table the way a card player might, face down, as though the argument underneath could still change. The assignment from Ms. Tan was due in three days: a debate on whether a parliamentary system or a presidential system did a better job of choosing and removing a head of government. He had drawn the parliamentary side, which he suspected was the harder one to defend, and Jiya had drawn the other, which meant she would be sitting across from him on Thursday with a prepared smirk.

His mother was on furlough from the plant until the new year, so she was home in the afternoons, moving between the living room and the kettle in a way that made the house feel both full and idle. "You want tea?" she asked, and when he shook his head she expostulated gently, saying a boy who studied that hard on a Saturday ought to at least drink something warm, and set a mug down beside his elbow anyway.

Jiya arrived at four with her laptop under her arm and a plastic bag of mandarins she proceeded to peel and divide without asking whether anyone wanted any. She wanted the debate to be good, genuinely good, not the usual recitation of talking points their class usually produced. She had told him in the hallway that she was tired of winning on style alone, and she had proposed this strange arrangement: they would prep together at his house, share sources, and keep nothing back.
