Tyson had agreed before he thought about what keeping nothing back would cost him.

"You go first," she said, dropping onto the chair across the table. "Convince me. How does a parliament even pick the leader?"

"The party with the majority does, or a coalition. The head of government isn't elected separately by the people the way a president is. The parliament makes and can unmake them." He said it and heard how thin it sounded, like a rule from a rulebook with no example attached. Jiya's expression told him the same thing.

"That's your problem," she said, not unkindly. "You're being cerebral about it. You've got the machinery but no story. I can say the president is elected by the whole country and removed only through impeachment, which barely ever works, and everyone in the room will picture something. What does your side look like?"

Tyson turned one of his cards over and found he had written nothing useful on it. He typed Germany into the search bar because Germany was the example Ms. Tan had circled on the assignment sheet, the country he had been assigned to research. His mother, passing behind him with her tea, glanced at the screen and said, "Kohl. I remember him. The big one. He was chancellor for years and years."

Jiya leaned in. "So he won elections."

"That's what I'm checking," Tyson said, and the pace of everything slowed for him then, the way it does when you sense you are near something before you can name it. He scrolled. He found a page about German chancellors and began reading down the list, Schmidt, Schmidt, Schmidt, and then 1982, and then Kohl. He read the line twice. Then a third time, because he could not make it behave like the other facts he had gathered.

"Listen to this," he said, and his voice came out quieter than he meant it to. "In 1982 Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as German chancellor through something called a constructive vote of no confidence." Jiya frowned at the phrase. "And it's the only time the procedure has succeeded at the federal level."

"So there was no general election," Jiya said slowly, testing it. "The country woke up with a different leader and nobody voted for the change." She sat back, and Tyson watched her weigh it, watched her see both edges of the blade at once. It was the weakness of his side and the strength of it, packed into a single sentence: a parliament could remove a head of government without waiting for an election, but it could also install one the voters had never directly chosen.

He took a breath and tried to hold both thoughts at once, which was harder than taking a side. "I think that's my argument, but honest," he said. "The German system, at least, makes removal possible and makes it rare. Impeachment in a presidential system is like a door painted on a wall. The constructive vote is a real door that almost nobody walks through." Jiya was already typing, and when he asked what she was doing she turned the laptop so he could see: she was taking down the exact same fact, the same date, the same two names, for her own notes. "You said share sources," she said. "I'm keeping my word."

His mother called from the kitchen that the kettle was on again, and Ms. Tan, who lived two doors down and had been out walking her dog, knocked at the screen door to return a casserole dish, and was persuaded to come in and take a chair. "How's the debate?" she asked, and Tyson slid the notes across to her. She read for a long moment without expression.

"Which side are you on?" she asked.

"Thursday I'm on the parliamentary side," Tyson said. "I still don't know which one I actually believe." Ms. Tan handed the notes back, and Jiya was already peeling another mandarin, laying the segments in a neat row along the edge of the table like evidence she had not yet decided how to use.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back in student housing found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends.
story:
The truck's passenger seat had been Nathan's for six hours, and by the sixth hour he had memorized everything wrong with it: the broken armrest, the smell of the mover's blanket folded under his feet, the radio that only caught one station clearly, an antiquated country channel his father insisted on keeping low. Between his sneakers sat a shoebox holding everything he refused to let the movers pack, which was to say the evidence of a life: ticket stubs, a bent wristband from the fall fair, three notes passed in Ms. Byrne's class and never thrown away.

They had left at dawn, before anyone else on his street was awake, because his father said goodbyes at noon were worse. Nathan had disagreed with that at the time. Ally had shown up anyway, at six in the morning, standing on the curb in her soccer jacket while the movers slid his dresser up the ramp. She hadn't cried, which somehow made it harder.

"You're going to hate it," she had said.

"I'm not going to hate it. That's not even a real prediction."

"It's a real prediction. You hate new things. You hated the new math teacher for a month."

"She was bad at math."

"You hated the new mall for a month, Nathan. It's a mall."

He had laughed then, and the laugh had cost him something, and he'd gotten in the truck before it could cost him more.

Now his father drove with both hands on the wheel, doing that thing where he pretended the silence was comfortable. Nathan looked at the shoebox, then out the window at a town he'd never see again, and pulled out one of Ms. Byrne's notes. It was from the last week of school, written on the back of a handout about a study she'd made them read, three psychologists named Festinger, Schachter and Back, from 1950. He'd thought it was boring then. He'd written a paragraph about it for the exam and forgotten it.

The note was from Mathys. It said: did you do the reading? is it saying friendship is just about where you live?? that's depressing as hell. Nathan turned it over. Below the handout's summary he found his own handwriting, the part he'd copied down because it seemed strange: the study was done in student housing, and it found that people living closer together, or near the shared stairways, were more likely to become friends.

He read it twice, and then he got angry, quietly, at a document in a shoebox.

" Dad," he said. "Did you pick the new house, or did the job pick it?"

"The job picked the town. I picked the house."

"Why that one?"

His father shrugged. "Good street. Other kids on it, the realtor said. You want lunch at the next exit?"

Nathan didn't answer. Because the answer to the real question, the one he couldn't ask, was sitting in his lap: maybe the job had picked his friends, not him. Maybe he hadn't chosen Mathys at all; maybe in grade eight their lockers had just been twelve feet apart and everything after that was stairways. That felt like a theft. He'd always thought of friendship as something you were enfranchised to, a vote you cast, and the study seemed to say the voting was rigged by floor plans. Even the grief he was carrying seemed suddenly misdelivered, a package with the wrong apportionment of blame, some of it owed to geography instead of his father.

He was still holding the note when his phone buzzed against his thigh.

Ally: ok I read the thing. the 1950 study. mathys sent it to me last night.

Nathan typed: and?

Ally: and I hated it. then I thought about it all night. every single person I'm close to, I see constantly. like it's all just, who's near the stairway.

Nathan: I know. I've been sitting here with the same note for an hour.

Ally: but here's the thing. you and mathys had lockers near each other. I didn't. I met you in line for the photo day and I chose to keep talking to you. so it's not all stairways.

He stared at that for a long time, watching the guardrails tick past. It didn't settle anything. Maybe proximity started things and something else kept them, or maybe Ally was wrong and she only thought she'd chosen him, or maybe the truth was some mixture he couldn't split cleanly, and he would have to live in that not-knowing for a while. The study was still true. So was the line at photo day. Both things could be true at once, and no one had ever told him that was allowed.

He put the note back in the shoebox and set the box on his knees, holding it there with both hands like something that could still change its mind.

"Lunch at the next exit," he said. "But I'm choosing the place."

His father glanced over, and something in his face eased, just at the corners. "Deal."

Nathan texted Ally one more thing before the exit sign came up: same time zone. I checked.

She sent back a thumbs up, and then: two hours. he's two hours ahead, mathys says. time zones don't work like you think.

He looked it up. Mathys was right.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: The DASH diet, short for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension, was tested in a US trial funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and published in 1997.
story:
Marcus had signed up for the junior medic track at Camp Wanawana because his mother said it would look good on applications, and because his grandfather had come home from the cardiology clinic in June with a folded sheet of paper he kept losing. Marcus was the only one in the family who had read the sheet. It listed a diet the doctor had named, a word Marcus had copied onto his palm in pen before the bus left.

The medic track met in the infirmary porch, six campers and Ms. Gauthier, the nurse, who was choleric on the subject of horseshoe games played near her stretcher. The first week they learned to wrap bandages. The second week she brought out the blood pressure cuff, an old manual one with a dial like a clock face, and made each of them pump it up on a partner's arm until the dial swung and fell.

"You're listening for two sounds," she said. "The first one is the top number, the pressure when the heart pushes. The second is the bottom, when it rests. Write both. Never write just one."

Marcus practiced on Daphnee, who narrated the tightening of the cuff as though she were being abducted by aliens, and on Ria, who sat still as a post and asked why the dial jumped around. "Because the arm moves," Ms. Gauthier said, "or because you're moving the stethoscope. The reading is honest. You're the unreliable part."

That night, in the tent, Marcus looked at the word inked sideways across his palm. He had one bar of signal by the picnic table. He typed the word in and found that it was an acronym: Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. Hypertension, high blood pressure, the thing the numbers on his grandfather's sheet were about. There was more on the page about a trial, a big one, funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and published in 1997. He read it twice, then the battery dropped to five percent and the screen went grey.

He wrote a letter instead, by flashlight, on the camp stationery with the loon on it.

Dear Grandpa, I know what the diet is called now. DASH stands for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. It isn't a brand or a person, it's what the letters mean. It was tested in a real trial, a big one, paid for by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the results were published in 1997, so it isn't something somebody made up last week to sell cookbooks. I'm learning to take blood pressure at camp so I'll check yours when I get home, if you want. You have to sit still and not talk. I know that's hard for you. Love, Marcus.

He read it over. It sounded like he was proselytizing, the way people did about keto at the Thanksgiving table, and he didn't want that. He crossed out a sentence about salt and rewrote it as a question, asking what the doctor had actually said, then crossed out the question too and left the page plainer than he liked.

The next morning he mailed it at the camp store, where the cashier weighed it and charged him a stamp.

Ria found him at the picnic table with the stationery. "You wrote a letter? Like, on paper?"

"My grandpa doesn't do texts."

"What's he got?"

Marcus explained the numbers, the top and the bottom, what high meant in general terms, that the diet was what the letters said it was, tested in a trial, published in 1997. Ria said her father had one of those wrist machines at home and nobody in the house believed it.

"People believe what they want," Marcus said. "That's the problem. My grandpa thinks if the diet were real, his doctor would have explained it better."

"Maybe the doctor explains it fifty times a day," Ria said.

The last week of camp, Ms. Gauthier let them run the blood pressure station at the camp health fair. Marcus took eleven readings, and the eleventh was the camp director, whose top number came out high enough that Ms. Gauthier retook it herself and wrote it on a card and told him to see his own doctor. The director laughed, the loud laugh of a man not laughing at anything, and took the card anyway.

Marcus watched him walk off with it. He thought about the letter, which was somewhere in a sorting facility by now, and about his grandfather reading Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension on loon stationery and possibly setting it under a magnet. There was a version of this where the diet worked, and a version where his grandfather followed it like an asceticism, refusing birthday cake and breakfast sausages out of pure fear, and Marcus did not know which version was more likely, or whether a grandson's letter could tip it either way.

Ms. Gauthier packed the cuff into its case. "You," she said to Marcus, "had the steadiest hands of the group. You weren't squeezing the bulb like you were strangling it."

He helped her carry the table back to the infirmary. Two days later there was a letter in his mailbox at the camp office, his grandfather's cramped hand on the envelope, thin enough to hold a single page. Marcus stood under the eaves where the rain came off the roof in a line, and turned it over, and put it in his back pocket unopened, to read on the bus with his full attention.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: In a fixed-payment loan, each payment's interest is charged on the remaining balance, so early payments go more toward interest and later payments more toward principal.
story:
The sedan on the far end of the lot was the cheapest thing with four wheels, and William had walked past it twice already as though that made him a serious buyer. Rayyan trailed behind him, hands in his pockets, offering commentary. "You could get a bike," he said. "You could get, like, six bikes."

"I need a car for the job. The job is twenty minutes away. The bike was fine for school."

"Mr. Tanaka's going to eat you alive in there."

Mr. Tanaka was the finance manager, a small neat man whose desk was arranged with the care of a shrine. He had already burned the word "payment" into the conversation the way a jeweler burnishes silver, polishing it until it shone: monthly payment, down payment, first payment deferred. William had saved two thousand dollars from two summers of bagging groceries, and he was proud of it, though he was beginning to suspect that pride was the cheapest thing he'd brought in.

"There's a graduation incentive," Mr. Tanaka said, sliding a folder across the desk. "Very munificent of the manufacturer, if I say so. Twelve hundred off, plus the rate you see there."

William looked at the rate and then at the payment, and the payment was a number he could actually afford, which was the trap, he suspected, though he couldn't say how. "How long is the loan?"

"Seventy-two months. Very common for a first car."

Rayyan leaned over and murmured, "Six years. You'll be a different person. You might have a beard."

The printout inside the folder showed the schedule, all seventy-two rows of it, and William ran his finger down the columns while Mr. Tanaka answered a phone call. First payment: a number under interest, a smaller number under principal. Second row: slightly less interest, slightly more principal. He kept going, and somewhere around row twenty he stopped and did the arithmetic on the back of a receipt. His first payment, of the money actually leaving his pocket, would take barely a hundred dollars off what he owed. The rest was interest, charged on the balance still remaining, which was almost all of it.

When Mr. Tanaka hung up, William pushed the paper back toward him. "So at the start, most of the payment is interest."

"That's correct. On a fixed-payment loan, the interest each month is charged on the remaining balance. Early on, that balance is large, so early payments go more to interest. Later payments, more to principal." He said it pleasantly, the way a man says something he has said four hundred times.

"So if I paid it off early, or if I sold the car in a year, I'd have paid all that interest and barely touched the price of the car."

"That's the structure of it, yes."

William sat back. The sedan was a good car. He had wanted it with a specific, physical wanting, and the wanting was still there, sitting beside him like a passenger. But the schedule had changed its shape. Six years of payments arranged so that the money he could least spare, the early money, the money from the entry-level version of himself, did the least work. And meanwhile his two thousand dollars, if it stayed in the savings account his mother had opened for him, earned interest itself, compounding quietly in the other direction, small and patient the way the loan was large and impatient.

"I have cash," he said. "Two thousand. What does that do to the schedule?"

"It shortens it. Or lowers the payment. Or both, depending."

"Can I see the new schedule before I decide anything?"

Mr. Tanaka regarded him for a moment, and then, instead of the salesman's smile, he gave him something more like respect. He turned to his keyboard. "You know, most people don't read the folder."

"My friend Rayyan reads everything," William said. "It's contagious."

"He sounds like an ascetic," Mr. Tanaka said, and Rayyan, offended, said, "I had a milkshake today, actually," which settled nothing.

The printer hummed and produced a new sheet. William took it and read it slowly, and there were things in it he still couldn't see clearly, the resale value, the insurance, the whole fogged future of six years in which he would become someone he couldn't yet predict. But he could see the first row. He put his finger on it.

"Okay," he said. "Tell me about the shorter one."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: CIRCLE, a research center at Tufts University, estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election.
story:
Jason turned eighteen on the fourth of October, which meant the November ballot would be his first, and he had promised himself he would decide before the line at the polling place decided for him. The decision had a way of sequestering itself at the back of his mind during school hours, then escaping at odd moments, on the bus, in the shower, while Mr. Morningstar diagrammed supply curves on the whiteboard and Jason copied them without reading them. On Saturday he walked to the coffee shop on Mercer Street with his voter registration card folded into his jacket pocket like a letter he hadn't opened.

Sameer was already at the corner table, and Zayden came in two minutes later, shaking rain off his jacket and complaining about the weather in the tone of someone who wanted to be talked out of it. They had been meeting at this table since sophomore year, when it had been about video games, then about girls, then, gradually, about things that mattered more and were harder to say. Today Sameer had his laptop open to a news article he'd been reading, and he slid it toward the middle of the table before Jason had even sat down.

"Half of us don't even show up," Sameer said. "That's what I keep telling people. There's a research center at Tufts, CIRCLE, and they estimated that fifty percent of Americans aged eighteen to twenty-nine voted in the 2020 presidential election. Fifty. So we sit here arguing about candidates and half the people our age couldn't be bothered."

Zayden pulled his cap off and set it on the table. "So because half stayed home, the ones who show up matter less? That's backwards. If half of us stay home, then my vote counts double, basically. Every person our age who actually votes is speaking for two."

"That's not how it works."

"It's exactly how it works. If nobody like us votes, nobody campaigns for us, and then nobody like us votes. It's a loop." Zayden tapped the table twice, as if that settled it.

Jason wrapped both hands around his cup. He hadn't said anything yet, which for him was usual; he liked to let the argument run until it wore itself out and showed what was underneath. The problem was that he agreed with both of them. The turnout number embarrassed him, the way a bad grade from a class you actually cared about embarrassed you. At the same time, he understood Zayden's arithmetic in a visceral way, the sense that a vote cast by someone nobody expected to vote carried a small, irrational weight, like a coin dropped into a pond nobody thought anyone was watching.

"It's both," Jason said finally. "It's embarrassing and it's an opening. Those aren't opposites, they're the same fact pointed in two directions." He heard his own voice say it and wondered if it was actually a position or just a way of standing between his two friends without choosing.

"That's not a position," Sameer said, but he said it almost kindly, the way he said true things.

On Monday Jason went back to the coffee shop alone, after his shift bussing tables, and spent forty minutes on the shop's sluggish wifi with the sample ballot the county had mailed him. He looked up each race, the school board and the water district and the two ballot measures with their clauses buried like stones in a field. He didn't finish. The judge retention questions he simply could not make sense of, and he wrote in his notebook, still unclear, and felt the strange exhilaration of admitting it, because admitting it meant the rest of what he'd decided was actually decided, not guessed.

Zayden appeared at six, shaking rain off his jacket again, and sat down across from him uninvited. "Sameer's voting early tomorrow," he said. "His mom's driving him to the election office before work. I told him we'd meet him there."

"He didn't tell me that."

"He figured you weren't voting. Not because you said that, just, you never say anything."

Jason looked down at his notebook, at the column of names with checkmarks beside them, at the words still unclear at the bottom. "I'm voting Tuesday," he said. "I'm leaving the judge questions blank. I'm not going to pretend I understand them."

"Blank is allowed?"

"It's allowed. I checked."

Zayden leaned back and looked at him for a moment, and something in his face shifted, some assumption being quietly put away. "Okay," he said. "Tuesday." Then he stole one of Jason's fries off the plate Jason hadn't touched and asked him about the water district measure, and Jason slid the notebook across the table so they could read the language of it together, side by side, under the coffee shop's yellow light, while the rain kept on against the window.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Roger Tomlinson led development of the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s, the first computerized GIS, and is often called the father of GIS.
story:
The fan in his grandfather's study made a sound like a slow argument, and Aidan sat beneath it with the laptop his mother had lent him, layers of a city building themselves out of nothing. He was spending July here so his grandfather could recuperate from the surgery in peace, though "peace" was a generous word for a house containing a recovering man who objected to being brought tea he had not asked for. The software was the real reason he had come. Ms. Suryanto had shown the class one demo in the spring and then left the rest to them, and Aidan had decided, without announcing it, that he would teach himself to overlay flood risk on a map of housing before September.

He started with the river. The first layer was terrain, gray and dull, then the floodplain data the city published, which arrived as a blue wash over the low streets. When he added parcels, every house became a small polygon, and where the blue and the polygons coincided, the map told a story no one had written down in so many words. His grandfather's house sat on a hill, smug and dry, half a mile from the nearest blue.

"Are you playing a game?" his grandfather asked from the doorway, meaning it as a joke and also as an accusation.

"It's a map," Aidan said. "Sort of. You turn things on and off." He toggled the flood layer off and the whole east side of the city went quiet and beige, as if the water had never been a consideration.

His grandfather lowered himself into the chair beside him with the deliberateness of a man negotiating with his own ribs. "In my day a map was a map. It didn't flicker."

On Thursday Thierry came over, ostensibly to help with the project and actually to escape his own house, where his younger brothers had become obstreperous in the heat. He dropped into the chair still warm from the grandfather and peered at the screen. "That's GIS, isn't it. Ms. Suryanto mentioned it once." Then, with the particular authority of someone who had looked something up two days ago and retained it perfectly, he added, "Roger Tomlinson led development of the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s. First computerized GIS. They call him the father of GIS."

"Where did you read that?"

"An article. There was a photo of him." Thierry seemed to feel the photo was important evidence. "He looks like everyone's uncle."

Aidan typed the name into a search and found the same sentence repeated in different fonts, and it struck him that the thing he was doing in this fan-cooled room had a beginning, an actual person and decade, not the anonymous forever he had assumed. He had pictured the software the way he pictured the internet, as something that had always been there, like antiquity, like rivers. The fact that someone had built it, in Canada, on machines that filled rooms, made his laptop feel less like a window and more like an inheritance.

The work itself went less smoothly. The flood data was from 2011 and the parcels from 2019, and Thierry noticed it first: a subdivision on the east side sat squarely inside the blue, houses drawn over water that the older layer remembered. "So which one's true?" Thierry asked.

"Both, probably. The water's modeled, the houses are real. The question is what the model would say now."

"You could ask the city."

"The city will say what the city says." Aidan said it with more certainty than he had. He was beginning to understand that a map was not a verdict; it was an argument, and the overlay was only as honest as the layers and the years you chose to stack. He could show his grandfather's neighborhood as safe, or as threatened, or as irrelevant, depending on what he switched on.

His grandfather reappeared at four with two glasses of lemonade, which he set down without comment, and stood behind them for a long minute. On the screen Aidan had layered the blue wash, the parcels, and a census layer he had coaxed into pale oranges, so that the houses inside the floodplain glowed a shade warmer than the ones on the hill.

"What am I looking at?" his grandfather asked.

"Whose houses flood first," Aidan said. "If it floods."

His grandfather drank his lemonade slowly, looking at the east side of the city, at the small bright polygons clustered along the old riverbed. Then he set the glass down on top of a coaster he pretended not to need and said, "The Kerns lived down there. Before they built the embankment."

"Who are the Kerns?"

"Nobody, now." He tapped the screen once, gently, on a block where the orange was deepest. "Start there."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, and splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules for a net gain of two ATP.
story:
The retake was scheduled for Monday, which gave Colton four days to learn cellular respiration on a farm where the only mitochondria in sight belonged to a horse named Duke and a flock of chickens who had never once produced ATP on command. Ms. Visser had handed back his exam with a single note, see me, and then told him only that he could redraw the cell diagram from scratch, correctly, if he wanted the marks. The word "correctly" had carried a certain hegemony of its own, the kind wielded by people who controlled grade books, and Colton had signed the retake sheet without arguing.

He spread his notes on the tailgate of his father's pickup because the kitchen table was buried in seed catalogues and the barn was cooler anyway. The August heat enervated him by ten in the morning, flattening his concentration until the lines on the page seemed to swim, so he worked early, shirt stuck to his back, drawing a cell in his spiral notebook. Mitochondria went in the middle, big and bean-shaped, because that was the part everyone remembered. Then he drew an arrow labeled glycolysis, and without thinking twice, he put the arrow inside the bean.

Desirae found him there at noon, driving her grandfather's Gator up the lane with a binder on her lap. She was preparing a speech for the county competition on Saturday, about the hegemony of the big grain companies over small farms like hers, and she had appointed Colton her audience on the grounds that he was the only person she knew who would sit still. She was loquacious by nature and more so under deadline, which meant the barn sometimes felt like a radio station with one program. Today, though, she parked, climbed onto the tailgate, and looked at his notebook before he could close it.

"That's wrong," she said, pointing at the arrow.

"It's a drawing, not a painting. It's supposed to be approximate."

"It's in the wrong place. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria." She said it the way she said lines from her speech, flat and certain, and Colton sat with that for a second, because it had never occurred to him that the first step would be outside the engine. He flipped back through his notes, the ones he'd taken during a lecture he'd spent mostly drawing a different, better horse, and found Ms. Visser's slide half-copied: glycolysis, cytoplasm, one glucose split into two pyruvate. The part he had actually written down, in his own handwriting, was the net gain of two ATP, because the number two had seemed like something a test would want.

"So the glucose gets broken out there," he said slowly, tapping the space between his bean-shaped mitochondria and the edge of the cell, "and the pieces come in after."

"The pyruvate," Desirae said, checking her own phone, because apparently she had a higher grade in biology than he did and had never mentioned it in three years of friendship. "Two of them, from one glucose."

He erased the arrow and redrew it in the cytoplasm, then drew two smaller arrows carrying the pyruvate through the mitochondrial membrane like trucks through a gate. It was strange, he thought, working the pencil, that the cell would do its first work in the yard instead of the factory. Strange too that he had never noticed he believed otherwise, that his diagram had been a quiet little assumption rather than knowledge. He had always trusted the big labeled organelles to matter most, the way Desirae's speech said people trusted the big companies to feed them, and both trusts turned out to be about who got the ink.

"I owe you," he said.

"You owe me forty minutes of listening," Desirae said. "I'm on paragraph six and Grandpa fell asleep in the rocking chair before paragraph two."

She gave the speech leaning against the pickup's wheel well, half to him and half to Duke, who watched through the fence with what Colton chose to interpret as sympathy. Her argument was that the buyers set the prices and the farmers learned to accept them, and that this was quieter than a takeover and therefore harder to fight, and Colton found himself thinking about his own diagram again, the way a wrong arrow survives because nobody checks the small print. When she finished, she closed the binder and looked at him like a person waiting for a verdict that mattered more than the county judges.

"The paragraph about the grain elevators is the strongest," Colton said. "Say that one slower."

She nodded, opened the binder again, and Colton turned back to his page, where the two pyruvate sat outside the mitochondria like letters that hadn't been mailed yet, and drew the arrow in.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that everyone aged 13 to 64 be tested for HIV at least once as part of routine health care.
story:
The waiting room of Bright Smile Family Dental smelled like spearmint and hot printer toner, and Morgan had been sitting in it for forty minutes with a worksheet on her lap that she was supposed to turn into a fifteen-minute peer health workshop by Thursday. The worksheet said things like "Explain consent in your own words" and "List three clinic services," and so far her own words were "uh" and "like." Across the room, Kathy was reading a magazine upside down, which she claimed helped her prognosticate the horoscope, because the stars worked better scrambled.

"Your turn will come, Morgan," the receptionist sang out, in the tone of someone who had said it eleven times that morning.

"I'm not nervous," Morgan said, which was true about the dentist and false about the workshop. Her problem was simple and stupid: she'd volunteered to run the session because Annika had dared her, and now she had to stand up in front of thirty classmates and say words out loud about consent and contraception and getting tested, words she had never once said in a room that contained other humans. She practiced under her breath. "Consent is a, it's an ongoing, it's like when the hygienist asks if you're okay and you can say stop."

Kathy lowered the magazine. "That's actually not bad. The dentist version."

"Every dental appointment I've ever had, they ask before they poke. And you can change your mind mid-poke." Morgan tapped the worksheet. "Maybe that's my whole framework. This whole place is a consent workshop with better lighting."

Then they called her back, and the hygienist, a young woman with a shark tattoo on her wrist, said, "I'm going to put this little mirror in your cheek, okay? Tell me if it's uncomfortable, and we'll adjust. You're the boss of your mouth." Morgan, dripping into a paper bib, felt the ridiculous satisfaction of a theory confirmed. When the suction wand buzzed to life she raised her hand and the hygienist switched it off immediately, no questions, and that tiny transaction felt like a demonstration more convincing than anything on the worksheet.

Dr. Okafor came in, pronounced her wisdom teeth "not yet a problem, but I prognosticate one," and then, while flipping a glove on, said, "While you're here, we also offer a rapid HIV test. Oral swab, takes a minute. The CDC recommends everyone aged thirteen to sixty-four be tested at least once as part of routine health care, so we make it routine here."

Morgan sat up so fast the suction wand clattered into its holder. "Wait. Here? At the dentist?"

"Swab along the gum, results in twenty minutes, and you can say no. Routine doesn't mean mandatory." He held up the swab like it was a tiny scepter. "Want it?"

She looked at the ceiling light, at the shark tattoo, at the paper bib with its cartoon tooth giving a thumbs-up. She thought about her workshop, where she was supposed to tell people where to get tested, and how she had been planning to say "a clinic," vaguely, as if clinics were mythical and located in fog. Here was a test being offered between a filling check and a free toothbrush. "Yes," she said. "Also, can I tell my class about this? Like, exactly this?"

The hygienist laughed. "We'll give you a pamphlet."

While the swab sat in her mouth, tasting faintly of plastic and salt, Morgan texted Annika under the edge of the chair: found out you can get an hiv test at the DENTIST. it's routine. cdc says everyone 13 to 64 at least once. Annika replied with nine exclamation points and the message "kathy owes me five dollars," which explained, Morgan realized, why Kathy had been so calm about the horoscope. They had prognosticated her.

The twenty minutes she spent waiting, she used. On the back of the worksheet she wrote "lemma," because that was what the session actually was, in the math sense: a small thing you prove first so the big thing becomes easy. Lemma one: your body, your call, stated out loud, asked before any touching, revocable at any moment, including by raised hand through a mouthful of suction wand. Lemma two: contraception, which she still had to research, and which she underlined twice with a self-directed sternness. Lemma three: testing, which was not a punishment or a confession but a thing so ordinary the dentist offered it beside the floss talk. The only part she still found wobbly was how to say "ongoing" without sounding like a textbook, and she wrote in the margin, "ongoing = you can stop mid-poke," which was perhaps the least elegant sentence she had ever produced and also the most tenable.

"Negative," Dr. Okafor said, coming back in. "For the record, that's the result we prognosticate for most people your age, which is rather the point of routine. Now open wide, because you have a spot on that left molar that I'd like to interrogate."

"Can I quote you in my workshop?" Morgan asked, around the mirror. "The routine part, not the interrogating part."

"Quote the pamphlet," he said. "It's more lawyer-approved."

At the front desk, the receptionist handed her a toothbrush, a sticker of a dancing molar, and the pamphlet, and Morgan walked out into the parking lot holding all three like evidence. Kathy was already waiting by the car, holding out her palm for the five dollars, and Morgan instead slapped the pamphlet into it. "You have to come to my workshop," she said. "You're the demo. Sit in the front row and I'll practice asking permission before I poke you with a pointer."

Kathy looked down at the pamphlet, then up, grinning. "Only if I get to say stop."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guideline, normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic.
story:
The bathroom had become Dylan's study, which his mother tolerated because it was the one room with a lock. The cuff came from the pharmacy on Route 9, and the chart, torn from the booklet, hung taped to the mirror beside the toothpaste. His father was upstairs, three weeks into a convalescence the doctors kept describing in language designed to sound calm, and Dylan had volunteered for a project he didn't yet know how to do: learn to read a blood pressure number, and explain to a classroom how a person could move it.

He practiced on his own arm first, pumping the bulb, watching the needle settle. One hundred eighteen over seventy-six. He copied it onto an index card, then checked the booklet. Under the guideline the class was using, the one from the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association, normal for an adult meant below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. He said it aloud until it stopped sounding like a password. Normal is under 120 and under 80. He was under both, barely, and the bareness of it bothered him in a way he couldn't have explained to anyone.

Eugenie knocked at four, holding a bag of chips she'd clearly brought as a peace offering, since they hadn't spoken since he'd told Mr. Tang he'd rather work alone. "Judith says you have a real cuff," she said through the door. "I want in. I need this grade, Dylan, and you need somebody who can actually talk to a room."

He let her in. She sat on the edge of the tub, sullen about the chips he'd confiscated, while he wrapped the cuff around her upper arm and told her to stop talking. The bathroom went quiet except for the Velcro and the hiss.

"What's the number?" she asked.

"One forty-two," he said, and stopped. "Over ninety-four."

She laughed, one syllable, and then saw his face and stopped laughing. "That's bad, right? That's the bad zone."

He didn't answer, because he was doing the arithmetic against the chart and the arithmetic kept coming out the same. Above 120. Above 80, well above. He took the cuff off her arm gently, the way you'd put down something that had turned out to be fragile, and said, "Sit still. Don't move." He took it again. One hundred forty. Over ninety-two.

"That machine cost nineteen dollars," Eugenie said. "It's probably broken."

"It measured me fine an hour ago."

"So measure Judith."

Judith was downstairs helping his mother with the laundry, which she did on Saturdays without anyone asking, a habit so steady nobody commented on it anymore. Dylan called down and she came up, wiping her hands on her jeans, and squeezed into the bathroom with the two of them. Ninety-eight over sixty-four. Eugenie exhaled. Dylan wrote it down, then sat on the closed toilet lid and looked at the three numbers in his notebook: his, Judith's, Eugenie's.

"Mr. Tang," Judith said suddenly. "At the pharmacy. He's got one of those proper machines by the counter, the kind with the chair. We could check it against his."

"That's not the machine," Eugenie said. Her voice had gone flat, the performance drained out of it. "Dylan. Is it the machine?"

He had learned, over the past hour of reading, that the number was a conversation between two forces, and that a person could change the conversation, that salt and sitting still and walking could all push it one direction or another, that this was the whole reason his project existed. But the booklet was careful to say that one reading was not a diagnosis, that machines erred, that a person could be frightened in a bathroom and produce a number that lied. He held both ideas at once, the way you hold two doors open, and found he could not make them into one clean sentence.

"I don't know," he said. "That's the honest answer. One reading isn't enough to know anything. But it's enough to know you should find out."

Eugenie looked at her arm, at the faint red stripe the cuff had left, as if the number were written there under the skin. "My mom's on pills for this," she said. "She never told me what for. I just found the bottle."

The rain that had threatened all afternoon finally arrived, hammering the small window, and for a moment nobody in the bathroom moved. Judith said, "The pharmacy's open till nine. Mr. Tang does readings for free, he likes the company."

Eugenie stood up and pulled her jacket off the hook, the one she'd hung with exaggerated care when she came in, back when she was still performing. "Fine," she said. "But you're both coming. If it's still high, I want it high in front of witnesses, because I am not telling my mother alone."

Dylan folded the chart off the mirror and put it in his pocket, next to the index card with his own number on it, 118 over 76, which no longer looked like such a comfortable place to live. He turned off the bathroom light. "Get the chips," he said. "We're taking them."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In C major the dominant seventh chord is G7, made of the notes G, B, D and F, and it pulls strongly toward the C major chord.
story:
The community centre kept its piano in a back room that smelled of floor wax and old coffee, an upright so anachronistic against the laminated posters about summer programs that Emma felt she had to touch it gently, as if it might object to the century it had landed in. She spread her manuscript paper on the bench beside her. Sixteen bars, quarter note equals ninety-two, a melody she had been carrying in her head since Tuesday and which had started, the moment she wrote it down, to sound like something from a hotel lobby. Mr. Lavoie had given them three weeks and one rule: the final bar had to feel finished. Hers did not. It ended the way a sentence ends when the speaker has simply stopped talking.

She played it through again, and again, and the beige carpet stretching toward the vending machines offered no opinion. Mr. Lavoie was somewhere down the hall with the drama group, and he had made it clear he would not listen to drafts. "You'll find it or you won't," he'd said, which Emma had privately decided was a thing adults said when they didn't know either.

The door opened and Kelly-Ann came in with Matilda behind her, both of them still holding the plastic cups from the front desk. "Is that it?" Kelly-Ann said, meaning the melody. "Play it." She set her cup on the lid of the piano, which Matilda moved immediately to the floor, and leaned on the instrument's shoulder the way she leaned on everything, as though the world owed her a wall. Kelly-Ann played clarinet and had once told Emma, without cruelty, that a weak ending could eviscerate an otherwise decent piece, that it made the listener feel robbed. Emma thought about that word now, robbed, while her fingers found the last four bars again.

"That's it?" Kelly-Ann said when the final chord, a plain C major with nothing before it but more C major, died in the carpet.

"It's finished," Emma said. "It just doesn't sound finished."

"Bar fifteen," said Matilda, who had come around the side to look at the page. Matilda hardly ever spoke first, and both of them turned. She pointed at Emma's chord above the second half of bar fifteen, a G major, G and B and D, which Emma had written because those were the notes her left hand had found. "Your top line is on F there," Matilda said. "Your chord isn't."

Emma looked. The melody note above that chord was an F, sitting outside the three notes she had written, a guest she hadn't seated. She had done it because the F was where the tune wanted to go and she hadn't wanted to argue with the tune. She wrote the F into the chord, making four notes: G, B, D and F.

"Play it," Kelly-Ann said.

Emma played bars thirteen through sixteen, and the last chord of fifteen, the one with the F added, reached toward the final C major chord like a hand reaching for a doorknob it already knew was there. All three of them heard it. Nobody said anything for a second, and then Matilda, still reading over Emma's shoulder, said, "G, B, D and F. That's G7. In C major they call that the dominant seventh. It pulls toward C."

"That's the whole thing," Kelly-Ann said. "That's what he wants."

From where Matilda stood, half behind the piano, she could see the page and Emma's face at once, and she watched Emma's pencil hover over bar fifteen without moving. Matilda had known the chord since she was nine, from her grandmother's hymn book, and she had learned early that the trick was everywhere, that half the songs on the radio were this one motion wearing different clothes. What she had not learned was why some people got to the trick and then stopped, dissatisfied, the way Emma was stopping now.

"You don't like it," Matilda said.

"It works," Emma said slowly. "It works so well it's almost boring. It's like every song I've ever heard." She played the four bars again, the G7 reaching, the C resolving, clean and inevitable. Then she played a version where she kept the F in the chord but delayed the resolution, holding the melody's last note over the bar line so the pull was there and the arrival was late. Kelly-Ann's eyebrows went up. It was stranger. It was also, possibly, worse. Emma looked at the two versions written now on the page, one above the other, and did not cross either one out.

Mr. Lavoie put his head in the door, saw the manuscript crowded with notes, and withdrew again without a word. Emma picked up her cup from the floor, took a swallow of cold coffee, and set her pencil down on bar fifteen, right between the endings.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Deliberate practice means working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, which improves skill more than simply playing through pieces already known.
story:
Peyton had been playing the Chopin waltz for eleven minutes when Ms. Augustin reached over and lifted the fallboard, quiet as closing a book. The studio smelled of rosin and the lavender hand cream Ms. Augustin kept by the metronome, and outside, someone was mowing a lawn two houses down.

"No," Ms. Augustin said. "Not today."

"You said I could keep it in my repertoire."

"I said you could keep it. I didn't say you could hide in it." She set the score of the Beethoven on the stand and turned to the second page, where two bars had defeated Peyton for three weeks. The left hand leapt a tenth and then had to land soft, and Peyton's wrist locked every single time. "These two bars. That's the lesson."

"That's, like, four seconds of music."

"That's, like, the only four seconds you can't play."

Peyton stared at the bars as though they had personally stigmatized her. At school, in front of Lyra and Fiona, she was the girl who played piano, the girl who had performed at the winter assembly, and Lyra had already told half the juniors that Peyton was auditioning for the regional youth orchestra in April. If she bombed the Beethoven, everyone would know what she actually was, which was a girl who could play one waltz and a lot of chords.

She tried the bars. Her wrist locked. She tried again and hit the wrong note, and again, and the mowing outside stopped and started and stopped, and the silence between her attempts got heavier.

"Play them six times," Ms. Augustin said, "and record them on your phone. Listen between takes. You'll hear what I hear."

"That's it? No demonstration?"

"I demonstrated last week. You watched my wrist and said, understood. You were watching my hands the way you watch the waltz. Like an audience."

At home that evening, Peyton put her chemistry homework on the music rack, propped open to the enthalpy diagrams she was supposed to be memorizing, and told herself she would drill after one more problem. The diagram showed a reaction climbing a hill before it could release energy, and she copied the little curve into her notes without really looking at it. Then she opened the waltz instead and played it through twice, the whole thing, beautifully, the way she always could.

It felt like nothing.

That was the part she couldn't explain to Fiona, who had texted, "aren't you basically already good?" Peyton sat with her hands in her lap. It had seemed axiomatic that playing well meant practicing what you played well, and the waltz sounded so good, so finished. But it had sounded exactly like this last month. She had the recording on her phone to prove it, a video from September that she'd watched last night, and the waltz was identical, note for note, no better, which meant the eleven minutes today had added up to zero.

She propped the phone on the lamp, set it to record, and opened the Beethoven to the two bars. She gave herself a goal, an actual goal, not "get better" but land the tenth soft, six takes. The first take she listened back and heard the thud she'd never noticed while playing, the impact of her left hand arriving like a dropped textbook. Second take, smaller thud. Third, she heard it live and eased off before she even checked. Fourth take, soft landing, wrong note. Fifth, right note. Sixth take she played four times in a row because the soft landing had started to feel possible, and the phone's speaker confirmed it: the tenth arrived like the rest of the phrase, like it had always belonged there.

At Thursday's lesson she played the bars, then the page, then the whole exposition, and Ms. Augustin let her finish without lifting the fallboard once.

"There's a name for what you did this week," Ms. Augustin said, closing the score. "Deliberate practice. Six takes, listening back."

"It also works on enthalpy, apparently," Peyton said. "I did my chemistry homework the same way."

Ms. Augustin laughed, the short one she almost never spent. "Same girl, same method."

Peyton tucked the waltz's score into her bag, then took it back out and left it on the shelf by the window, spines out, where she could see it from the bench. "Can I play it once before I go? Just once."

"After the two bars. Ten takes. I'll be listening."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA advises refrigerating cooked food within two hours, or within one hour if the air temperature is above 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
Sadie laid five empty containers in a row on the counter, lids stacked beside them like small roofs, and tried to imagine a week inside them. In three weeks she would be in a dorm with a shared kitchen on the ground floor, and her mother had said, in the tone she used for facts she didn't want to argue about, that food poisoning was a bad way to start a semester. So Sadie had volunteered to learn the whole business now, in this kitchen, while the August light came through the window and the freezer hummed its one patient note.

The plan came first, her mother insisted, and the shopping second, and the cooking last of all, which was the opposite of how Sadie had always thought about food. You wanted something, you made it. But a week of meals meant working backward: chicken on Sunday could become soup on Tuesday only if you bought the carrots on Sunday too, and the lentils had to be soaked the night before they mattered. It felt like a kind of foresight she'd never been asked to practice, less like cooking than like chess, and it oddly enthralled her, this quiet arranging of future meals before anyone was hungry.

Ms. Silva, from next door, had come over ostensibly to return a pie dish, but she stayed, because Ms. Silva always stayed. She wanted, Sadie suspected, to be useful in a house where her opinions were still solicited, and she circled the kitchen offering them. "You'll want to cook in batches," she said, tapping one of the containers. "Cook once, eat three times. That's how I survived my first apartment, and how my mother survived forty years of shift work." She said it lightly, but there was a wistfulness underneath, the way she always talked about that apartment, and Sadie understood that the sagacity was partly a souvenir, offered to whoever would carry it.

The chicken went into the oven at four. While it roasted, Sadie chopped carrots badly and then slightly less badly, and found herself thinking about July, about the lake.

It had been the last trip before everything scattered. Felicia had brought a cooler and a confidence about food that turned out to be mostly confidence. By lunch on the second day they had cold pasta salad and fried chicken from a place near the launch, and by late afternoon the campsite was an open field of heat, the thermometer hanging in the shade of the picnic table reading ninety-two. Anne-Sophie, who was cautious by nature and had already announced she wanted to apply to medical school, said the leftovers from lunch should probably be thrown out before dinner. Felicia said that was wasteful and paranoid, that people ate mayonnaise at picnics all the time, that her family had never once gotten sick. "It sat out for like five hours," Anne-Sophie said. "So did the sun," Felicia said, and laughed, and the two of them looked at Sadie because she was the tiebreaker.

Sadie had said they were probably fine. She'd said it partly because Felicia's certainty was easier than Anne-Sophie's worry, and partly because she wanted the fried chicken. They ate it at dusk. Nobody got sick, which Sadie now understood proved nothing at all, and the argument had dissolved into cards and bug spray, unresolved, the way their arguments often were.

But Anne-Sophie had texted her a screenshot that night, from a food safety page, and Sadie had read it twice under her sleeping bag's dim flashlight and felt a small, specific embarrassment. The rule was plain: you refrigerate cooked food within two hours, or within one hour if the air temperature is above ninety degrees Fahrenheit, which was thirty-two degrees Celsius. Their campsite had been at ninety-two. Lunch had gone five hours in that heat, sitting out on the table in the sun. "You were right," Sadie had texted back, and Anne-Sophie had replied only with a thumbs-up, which somehow carried both forgiveness and the refusal to gloat, and Sadie had liked her more for it.

The chicken came out golden at five-twelve. Her mother was still at work, Ms. Silva had gone home with instructions to return for soup on Wednesday, and the kitchen was Sadie's alone with its heat and its smell of rosemary. She stood at the counter with the carving knife and the row of containers and the phone propped against the fruit bowl, and she did the arithmetic she now did automatically, the way she'd been doing it all month: it was five-twelve, the food was out of the oven and hot, and the two hours had started.

She carved the breasts off the bone, cubed some for Tuesday's wraps, shredded the rest into the stockpot for soup. Thecontainers filled one by one, and she pressed the lids down until they sealed with a small sigh. Half the chicken would cool on the counter and go into the fridge within the hour anyway, because the kitchen was warm and she didn't want to raise the temperature inside the refrigerator; that compromise was hers, reasoned out between the rule and the appliance, and she held it lightly, the way she was learning to hold most of her conclusions. Felicia would say she'd become paranoid. Anne-Sophie would say she'd finally developed sense. Both of them, she suspected, would be describing the same person.

She labeled each container with the day, carried three to the refrigerator, and set the fourth on the sill to cool, where the last of the daylight caught the steam rising off it. Then she wrote "chicken, Sunday" on the final lid, her handwriting small and deliberate, and put the pen down on the counter beside the thermometer her mother kept by the window. It read eighty-four. She looked at it a moment longer, watching nothing change, and then she set the timer on her phone for one hour.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Progressive overload means gradually increasing training demands, such as weight, distance or intensity, so the body keeps having a reason to adapt.
story:
Loic had done the same forty laps every Tuesday and Thursday since October, and by June his shoulders had stopped aching, his time had stopped dropping, and a kid two lanes over had started beating him without appearing to try. The kid's name was Yacine. He was fourteen and swam like something being poured.

"You've plateaued," Yacine said one evening, dripping beside Loic at the shallow end, entirely without malice. "You do the same distance at the same pace every week, right?"

"I do it well," Loic said, which even he heard was not the point. "Consistency. That's what the internet said. Discipline builds adaptation."

"It builds it once." Yacine shrugged, pulled his cap on. "Progressive overload, that's what my coach calls it. You gradually increase the demands, like the distance or the intensity, so the body keeps having a reason to adapt."

Loic wanted to argue with him, on principle, because being corrected by a fourteen-year-old in a rubber cap had a certain flavor to it. But he had been staring at the same interval times in his notebook since February, columns of identical numbers like a fence he'd built around himself, and the notebook had been trying to tell him something for months. He had been doing forty laps. Forty was the number. Forty was comfortable.

On Friday he sat in the bleachers with Raya, who was reading a biology textbook upside down in the sun, and laid out the problem. He had, he admitted, two voices in his head. One said the body was a machine and machines needed programmed stress, increases, planned rest days, warm-ups before hard sets. The other said he'd gotten fit doing what felt right, and feeling was data too. Raya turned the textbook right side up.

"So pick a week and test it," she said. "Write the program. Gradually increase the demands, like distance or intensity, whatever you want, and schedule the rest. Then you'll know which voice is lying."

"That's not how I'll know anything. One week tells you nothing."

"So plan it for longer than a week, genius."

The arbitration took him most of the weekend, because once he started planning he couldn't stop. He wrote a Monday warm-up of shoulder rotations and easy kick sets, a Tuesday main set of forty-five laps with the middle ten at a pace that frightened him slightly, a Wednesday of nothing but walking to the kiosk and back, a Thursday of fifty laps broken into intervals, a Friday swim he refused to look at twice, and a Saturday so restful it was almost querulous, a note reading "do not, under any circumstances, get in the water," as though his own body might file a complaint about idleness. Sunday he left blank and stared at the blankness for a while, then wrote "light." He kept the total honest: small increases, one thing at a time, never everything at once. It looked, on the page, less like discipline than like kindness with a schedule attached.

The first new Tuesday, he did his forty-five laps and the frightening middle ten and climbed out with his arms humming. The first new Thursday, he managed fifty and lay on the concrete for a while, watching the ceiling fan of light wobble across the bottom of the pool. Ms. Gupta, who guarded the deep end and had watched him swim the same forty laps all winter with the expression of a woman saving her opinions for later, came to collect the kickboard he'd left on the edge.

"You're different this week," she said.

"I'm running an experiment."

"On yourself?"

"Who else would sign the consent form?"

She laughed, one syllable, and went back to her chair.

By the third week he had stopped thinking of the increases as betrayals of his old routine, and started thinking of them as the routine, which was either a synthesis or a surrender, and he couldn't decide which, and had decided that was allowed. He still didn't know whether the second voice, the feeling one, had been wrong or just premature. He kept it on the schedule as a tiebreaker: if a planned set felt genuinely wrong, not hard but wrong, he could pull back and write down why. Some weeks it spoke up. Most it didn't. He wrote down both kinds.

The Saturday of the fourth week, he arrived at the pool with his "do not, under any circumstances" note folded in his bag, purely as a talisman, and found Yacine standing at the edge of the shallow end, holding his shoulder at an angle shoulders should not hold.

"Coach had me adding things all at once," Yacine said, wincing as the physiotherapist's van pulled into the lot. "Thought I'd skip the boring part."

"Which boring part?"

"The rest days." Yacine lowered himself onto the bench beside Loic and looked, for the first time all summer, his actual age. "Can you write me one of those plans? The kind with the blank Sunday?"

Loic took out his notebook, turned past the fence of identical numbers, and tore out the page.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Cheating out means an actor turns their body partly toward the audience, even while talking to another character, so their face and voice carry.
story:
The living room had been a living room until four o'clock, when John moved the couch against the wall and laid down a rectangle of masking tape on the carpet. Inside the tape was the stage. His mother had looked in from the kitchen, decided not to ask, and gone back to chopping onions.

"One act, forty minutes, performed in the gym on Friday," John had told Mr. Whitaker when he'd asked to direct it instead of acting. Mr. Whitaker had agreed with the laconic efficiency of a man who had watched students ruin easier things, and had said only, "Your job is what the audience sees. Not what you see."

That sentence sat in John's head all through the first rehearsal, mostly because he didn't understand it yet. Karlee sat on the couch with a clipboard, marking entrances. Ulysse, who had the lead, stood at the kitchen doorway that served as the upstage exit, waiting for John to tell him where to go.

"You walk to Dana's chair, you argue, you leave," John said. Dana's chair was a folding chair with a sweater draped over it, since the actress who would play Dana had the flu and her understudy was at a dentist appointment. Half the cast was furniture today. That, John supposed, was what rehearsals were: an archipelago of real performances scattered across a sea of empty chairs.

Ulysse walked, argued with the sweater, and left. John watched from where the audience would be, sitting on the floor beyond the tape line. He watched Ulysse walk, argue, and leave, and what he saw, mostly, was the back of Ulysse's head.

"Hold on," John said. "Turn around."

"I'm talking to Dana."

"I know. But I can't hear half your lines and I can't see your face at all. You're facing the chair the whole scene."

"That's where Dana is," Ulysse said, with the patience of someone who had been acting since middle school. "People look at who they're talking to."

"Then stand like this," John said, and got up onto the taped stage himself. He angled his body toward the imaginary audience, his feet planted a quarter turn from the chair, his face still inclined toward Dana. "You cheat out. It means you turn your body partly toward the audience, even while you talk to another character, so your face and voice carry."

Ulysse tried it. The position looked unnatural, John had to admit, a conversation conducted at an angle no real person would choose. But from the floor, past the tape line, the difference was immediate: Ulysse's eyes, the set of his mouth before the line, the way his voice enunciated clearly across the room instead of disappearing into the kitchen doorway. The scene had a face now.

Karlee looked up from her clipboard. "So every scene where two people talk, they're both half-turned toward the audience? Won't it look weird if anyone ever sits where the couch usually is?"

"That's the thing," John said slowly. "It's fake and it's real at the same time." He walked the rectangle again, thinking out loud, because Karlee was the kind of friend who let him. "The story is that they're alone together. But the truth is there's a gym full of people on Friday, and the theater has to serve both. The actors pretend they don't see the audience, and the audience pretends the actors aren't turned toward them." He stopped at the corner he had decided was downstage left, though he'd had to look up which corner that was. "Maybe that's what Mr. Whitaker meant. Directing isn't about what the scene feels like from inside it. It's about what it looks like from out here."

"Or maybe he meant something else entirely," Karlee said.

"Probably," John said. "But it's a good enough wrong answer to keep."

They ran the scene six more times. By the fourth, Ulysse was cheating out without being reminded, even adding a small variation, turning nearly full-front for the line "I never wanted this house," and snapping back toward the chair for "and you knew that." John hadn't asked for that. He wrote in the margin of his script: Ulysse does a thing on the house line, keep it?

He didn't know yet whether to keep the couch out for Friday or to push for real risers in the gym. He didn't know whether Dana's understudy would cheat out, or whether he'd have to show her the way he'd shown Ulysse, standing at the wrong angle himself until she laughed and copied him. There were forty minutes of play and he had blocked eleven.

At six o'clock his mother called from the kitchen that dinner was ready, and everyone peeled tape off the carpet. Ulysse took the corner of the rectangle closest to the door, Karlee took the rest, and John stood for a moment inside the flattened space where the stage had been, the light from the window coming across it at the low angle an audience would never see.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index.
story:
The food court smelled like fryer oil and cinnamon, and Arianna had her essay prompt facedown on the table as if it might bite. "Explain, with reference to actual policy, why central banks raise interest rates to slow inflation." Audrey-Ann slid a tray of nachos toward her and said the assignment was a trap, that if you wrote it straight you sounded like a textbook, and if you wrote it cleverly you sounded like you were dodging. Paxton, who wanted to be a paramedic and took economics only because it fit his schedule, said the whole thing was simple, and that simplicity was exactly why he'd fail.

"It's not simple," Arianna said. "I know the sentence. Rates go up, borrowing costs more, people spend less, demand falls, prices stop climbing. I can recite it. But I can't explain it, not to someone who doesn't already believe it." She tapped the prompt. "My dad asked me last week why the Bank of Canada would deliberately make his mortgage renewal hurt, and I had nothing. I just stood there feeling like a fraud."

Paxton tore through his nachos with the efficiency of a man who ate only to refuel. "So fake it. Teachers can't tell the difference between understanding and a good vocabulary."

"That's a compliment," Audrey-Ann said, "to someone else."

Ms. Yilmaz, who taught at their school and was, inconveniently, eating alone two tables away, was reticent by reputation, the kind of teacher who answered questions with questions and let you stew. Arianna had been avoiding her since the essay was assigned, mostly out of pride, partly out of fear that Ms. Yilmaz would ask her something she couldn't answer in front of witnesses. Now she watched the older woman fold a napkin into smaller and smaller squares and decided that pride was cheaper than failing.

"Give me a scenario," Arianna said to Paxton, standing. "Something I can't dodge."

"Runaway inflation," Paxton said immediately. "Zimbabwe. Wheelbarrows of cash. Explain how a rate hike fixes that, and why it doesn't just wreck everyone with a loan."

She walked over. Ms. Yilmaz looked up before Arianna finished arriving, which was unnerving, and said, "The essay. Sit. You've been circling my classroom like a hawk that's afraid of mice." Arianna sat. She laid out her problem, the recited sentence, the father at the kitchen table, the fraudulent feeling that had begun to metastasize from that one bad night into a general suspicion of her own mind.

"You're missing an anchor," Ms. Yilmaz said. "You know the mechanism but not the destination. Ask yourself what number the whole machine is steering toward. When was it written down? By whom?" She picked up her tray and added, almost as an afterthought, "That's not the answer. That's the question that has one." Then she was gone, napkin square abandoned like a tiny monument.

Arianna came back to the table at speed. Audrey-Ann had her phone out already, because Audrey-Ann's own want that afternoon was a pair of boots on clearance and she'd been price-checking between bites. "Look up the Fed. Inflation target. When did they actually commit to a number?" Audrey-Ann's thumbs moved, then stopped. "Here. On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent." She scrolled. "Measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index." She looked up. "The P what?"

"Consumption expenditures," Arianna said slowly. "It's a price index. Different yardstick than CPI, doesn't matter why right now." She was staring at the date. 2012. The sentence she'd been reciting her whole life about cooling demand had a finish line drawn under it, and the finish line was drawn barely over a decade ago, after decades of the machine running without a stated destination. Her father hadn't been wrong to feel whiplashed. The target was young.

"So the whole essay is different now," Paxton said, watching her face change. "How?"

"Because before, I was defending the hike," Arianna said. "Rates up, pain for borrowers, prices calm, the end. A moral argument dressed as a mechanical one. Somebody has to absorb the cost and I couldn't say who without flinching." She pulled the prompt toward her. "But if the goal is two percent, explicit, on the record since 2012, then the rate hike is a steering correction, and the interesting question is who sits closest to the rudder when it turns. My dad's mortgage. People renewing this year. Not because anyone is cruel, but because the target is the target." She paused. "I still can't tell if that makes the central bank less culpable or more. That part might stay open."

"Put that in the essay," Audrey-Ann said. "The part you can't tell. Teachers eat that up."

"That's not why I'd put it in." Arianna wrote the date on the back of her hand, January 25, 2012, then the two percent beneath it, then the index, abbreviated because her wrist was only so wide. Paxton leaned over and read it upside down. "On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index," he recited, like a man reading a weather advisory, and shrugged. "Sounds like nothing happened."

"That's what makes it big," Arianna said. She capped her pen and stood, gathering the prompt, her notes, the nacho tray Paxton had demolished without appearing to eat. Audrey-ann was already three stores away, boots calling. At the escalator Arianna looked back once at the table where Ms. Yilmaz had sat, then pressed her wrist flat so the ink wouldn't smear, and rode up past the perfume counters toward the exit and the bus and the blank page waiting at home.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: For US federal Direct Subsidized student loans, the government pays the interest while the student is in school; unsubsidized loans build interest during that time.
story:
The financial aid letter had been sitting on Justin's desk for three days, sealed and then unsealed, folded and then unfolded, until the crease went soft. Tonight he finally carried it to the computer and typed the college's student aid portal into the browser, logging in with the password he'd written on a sticky note that his mother called an anachronism, since nobody wrote passwords down anymore. He was sixteen, a senior who had skipped a grade somewhere back in middle school, and the numbers on the screen were larger than any numbers he had ever been responsible for.

Abdallah was already in the video call window, his face lit blue by his own screen. "You opening it finally?" he said. "Carys said you'd chicken out until the deadline forced you."

"I'm not chickening out. I'm collating." Justin spread the letter's pages beside the keyboard: the cost of attendance, the grant, the work-study, and then two lines that looked almost identical except for one word. He read them aloud anyway, because saying them made them feel more real than seeing them. "Direct Subsidized Loan, five thousand five hundred. Direct Unsubsidized Loan, two thousand."

"Okay," Abdallah said. "So take both. Free money."

"It's not free. It's borrowed." Justin highlighted the word subsidized and stared at it, then opened a new tab and typed the whole phrase into the search bar. The results loaded, and he clicked the first one that wasn't an advertisement.

The page said it plainly, in the flat prose of a government website: for the subsidized loan, the government pays the interest while the student is in school. For the unsubsidized one, interest builds during that time, quietly, the way dust gathers on a windowsill nobody looks at. Justin read it twice, then a third time, moving his finger along the line on the screen the way he hadn't done since fourth grade.

"Wait," he said. "They're not the same thing at all. One of them sits there doing nothing while I'm in class. The other one's already growing."

Abdallah leaned closer to his camera. "Growing how? Like, right now?"

"I mean, not for me, I haven't taken it yet. But if I take it, then yes. Four years of it building before I even start paying it back." Justin pulled up the loan calculator the college itself provided, the one Mr. Holloway had mentioned back in the fall when he'd said, in his dry way, that every senior should open it at least once and flinch. Justin entered the amounts, the years, the rate they'd been assigned. The total at the bottom of the subsidized line stayed exactly what he'd typed in. The unsubsidized line climbed.

"Add the savings account thing," Abdallah said. "The one from your mom."

Justin had almost forgotten that part. His mother had opened a small savings account for him when he was ten, and every year she made him look at the statement so he could watch the interest land, tiny deposits he hadn't earned. "Same principle, opposite direction," he said slowly, typing the account number into the bank's site. There it was: the balance, and beneath it, a line of interest credited this month, more than the deposit he'd made from his summer job. Money sitting still could grow.
