Money borrowed could also grow, but it grew against you, and the only difference was which side of it you were standing on.

Carys joined the call five minutes later, out of breath, having run from somewhere. "Justin's back on the loan letter," Abdallah told her. "He relapsed. Classic recidivism."

"Shut up," Justin said, but he was smiling. "Carys, tell me if this is stupid. If I take the subsidized loan, the full five five, plus the grant, plus work-study, I might be able to skip the unsubsidized one entirely. Work more hours at Holloway's shop over the summer. Maybe not take the last two thousand at all."

Carys's face went thoughtful in the small window. "That's two thousand less in your pocket freshman year. You'd feel that. Books, the bus home."

"I'd feel the interest later, too."

"Later is later," she said. "I'm just saying it's a real cost either way. You're picking which one hurts."

Justin looked at the two lines on the letter again. He dragged his cursor across the word subsidized one more time, as if he could hold it. For four years, the government would stand between him and the growth of that debt, and that was worth something, maybe worth a harder summer, maybe worth a tighter first year. But he couldn't know yet what freshman year would cost him in ways no calculator listed. He thought of Mr. Holloway's shop, the smell of sawdust and machine oil, the hours stacking up at eleven dollars an hour.

"Okay," he said. "Subsidized, yes. Unsubsidized, I'm going to try to get through the first year without it, and I'll decide about year two when I get there. That's honest, isn't it? Not deciding is also a decision, but a smaller one."

"Write it down before you rationalize your way back," Carys said.

Justin opened a new document, typed the plan in two sentences, and printed it on the printer that groaned like it resented being woken. The page came out warm. He set it on the letter, then slid both into the folder his mother kept on the shelf above the desk.

"I'm going to email Holloway about summer hours," he said, and his fingers were already moving across the keys.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
story:
The country road outside town ran straight for two miles between fence posts and cut hay, and Thomas sat in the passenger seat of the driving school's small white car while Ms. Eze stood in the gravel drive with her clipboard, not moving. Maya was in the driver's seat, engine off, hands on the wheel, and Ms. Eze was saying, quietly, that the lesson would not begin. Thomas, fifteen minutes early for his own hour, leaned against the gatepost and tried to look like he wasn't watching. Maya's window was down. "I just forgot," she said. "We're in a driveway. We haven't moved an inch." Ms. Eze said that the driveway was exactly the point, that habits began before the key turned, and that she would wait all afternoon if she had to.

"She's being ridiculous," Thomas said later, when Maya had clicked the belt at last and the car had pulled out onto the road, and it was his turn in the seat. He said it lightly, the way he said most things, but Ms. Eze only adjusted the mirror on her side and told him to check his own belt before anything else. He found it already fastened; he had buckled it without thinking, because his father, a man who inculcated safety the way other men inculcated religion, had drilled it into him since he was four years old. He told her this, meaning it as a small joke at his father's expense. Ms. Eze did not laugh.

They drove. The road unspooled, and Thomas managed the clutch badly, stalled twice at the crossroads by the grain elevator, and then found a gear that held and a speed that felt like flying. The fields slid past, evanescent in the late light, gold going to grey, and he understood suddenly why his father loved driving, why anyone did. He was sixteen minutes into being a driver when Maya's little hatchback came the other way, passed them with her hand raised off the wheel, and disappeared around the bend where the road narrowed by the creek.

There was a sound after that. Not a crash, exactly. A sound like a large book dropped onto a floor, distant and dull, and Ms. Eze said one word, "Stop," in a voice Thomas had never heard from any adult, and he stopped the car, cleanly, in the middle of the road, and she was out the door before he had the handbrake up.

He walked the bend behind her. Maya's car sat angled into the ditch, its front end folded against a culvert, and Maya was standing beside it, one hand pressed to her collarbone, saying she was fine, she was fine, she was fine in a voice that got smaller each time. Ms. Eze held her by both shoulders and looked at her face, then at the windshield, which had a spidering of cracks on the passenger side. An old tractor had come out of the field lane, its driver saying, over and over, that he hadn't seen her, that the sun was in his eyes.

At the hospital, where they took Maya mostly to stop everyone arguing, a doctor with tired eyes examined her collarbone and told her it was bruised, not broken, and that she was lucky. Maya, sitting on the papered table, said, "The belt. She wouldn't start the lesson until I put it on." She said it as if confessing something, and Thomas, in the waiting area, heard her through the half-open door say, "I read somewhere that wearing a seat belt cuts serious crash injuries and deaths by about half." She said it slowly, like she was checking the arithmetic in her mouth.

Thomas sat with that. He had spent the drive composing the argument he would make, that rules imposed before the engine started were theater, that what mattered was judgment, was the actual road. But the belt hadn't been judgment. Maya hadn't decided anything in that driveway; she'd been made to do a thing she'd have skipped, and the thing had done its work an hour later without her choosing it. His father's way and Ms. Eze's way, which he'd filed under the same dull heading all his life, were suddenly two different animals: one a lecture, the other a shove that put you on the right side of a half. He couldn't yet say which he'd carry into his own driving, or whether they could be carried together, or whether the choice would ever really be his to make in the two seconds it mattered. He only knew that the argument he'd rehearsed was gone, and something unlabeled sat in its place.

Ms. Eze drove him home in the school car, the second lesson cancelled, both of them quiet. At his gate she stopped and looked over at him, and he expected a speech about what they'd seen. Instead she said, "You stopped well. When I said stop." He looked at the road behind them, already dark, where the culvert was, and said, "Same time next week?" She wrote it on the clipboard and handed him the slip of paper through the window.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Connecting words such as Spanish 'sin embargo', meaning 'however', let a debater signal a counterargument clearly even when the rest of their grammar is simple.
story:
The kitchen table at April's house had been cleared of everything except two textbooks, a plate of crackers, and Isabelle's phone, face down like a defendant. On the screen, when she dared to look, was the email from Mr. Bighorn: every student in Spanish III would debate a current issue for five minutes, entirely in Spanish, on Thursday. Five minutes. Isabelle had chosen the topic herself, whether the city should fund public transit over new highways, because she actually cared about it, and that was the problem. She cared in English. In Spanish she had the vocabulary of a small child and the argument structure of a shopping list.

"Bien," April said, tapping her pen against the table. "Start over. Empieza con el presupuesto."

"El presupuesto," Isabelle repeated. "El presupuesto es... es..." She gestured at the ceiling as if the next word might be stuck up there. "Grande?" She heard herself and put her head in her arms. "I sound like I'm describing a bear. The budget is big. The budget is bad. The budget is... a dog."

April laughed, but not unkindly, and Jaxson, sprawled on the living room floor with his own flashcards, called over without looking up, "Just say no a las carreteras a hundred times. That's a debate."

"That's a chant," Isabelle said into her sleeve.

They ran it again. Isabelle stood this time, because standing made her feel like someone who had prepared, and delivered her case: the highways cost too much money, the buses help many people, the pollution is bad for the city. Each sentence arrived alone, dragging the one behind it. She could hear the shape of it even through her clumsy accent, a pile of statements with no hinges between them, and when she finished, April hesitated in a way that told her everything.

"It's good," April said, "but it sounds like... a list? Like you're reading the reasons off your hand."

Isabelle sat back down. That was exactly it. In English she would have said however, on the other hand, even if the highway is faster, and the listener would hear her thinking, would hear her weighing one thing against another. In Spanish she had nothing but the reasons themselves, lined up shoulder to shoulder, and they debilitated each other by standing so close together. A person who argued like a list sounded like a person who hadn't considered the other side at all, and Mr. Bighorn's rubric, which she had read four times on the bus, had a whole line for engaging the counterargument.

"I need the glue," she said. "The words that connect." She pulled her laptop over and typed connecting words Spanish debate, and April leaned in beside her, chin on her hand, smelling faintly of the orange she'd eaten earlier. The screen filled with a list, and near the top of it, two words Isabelle had seen before in readings and never once used: sin embargo.

"What's it mean?" Jaxson asked, drifting over from the floor with his flashcards still in his fist.

"However," April said.

Isabelle tried it in her mouth. "Sin embargo." She looked back at the list, then at her own notes, where she'd written her arguments and, in smaller letters underneath, the objections she'd been planning to ignore. The opposition would say the highway saves time for commuters. Fine. Let them say it. "Los autobuses son lentos," she began again, slower now, hearing the sentence before she said it. "Sin embargo, el tren nuevo es rápido, y muchas personas no tienen carro." However. One word, and suddenly her five minutes had a shape, a bend in the middle of it, an acknowledgment that there was another side and that she had walked to the edge of it and come back carrying something.

They drilled until April's mother came home and started dinner, until Jaxson got bored and started quizzing them on animal names to feel useful, until the crackers were crumbs. Isabelle kept circling back to the same pivot, sometimes dropping it in too early, sometimes stacking it three times in a row like a nervous tic, and April kept shaking her head and saying otra vez. By the third run-through, Isabelle could feel where the turn belonged, in her body almost, the way she could feel a chorus coming in a song.

Thursday afternoon, Mr. Bighorn's classroom smelled like the radiator and somebody's vanilla lip balm. When he called her name, Isabelle stood, and across the room a boy who'd argued for the highway folded his arms, waiting for her list. She got through her first two reasons, saw him open his mouth, and took the turn before he could.

"Sin embargo," she said, "las carreteras nuevas son caras, y el presupuesto no es profligate." She paused, half a second, because she wasn't sure profligate was a word in Spanish, and decided it didn't matter, because Mr. Bighorn's eyebrows had gone up in a way that she chose to read as approval. The boy across the room lowered his hand.

"Three minutes forty," April mouthed from the second row, tapping her watch.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all cocoa butter with other fats, sets without tempering but does not have the same snap.
story:
The rain had been falling since noon, and Alexander stood in Kolton's kitchen with three bars of dark chocolate, a metal bowl, a thermometer borrowed from the garage, and four hours before Melyna's going-away party. She was leaving for a semester in Lisbon in six days, and he had decided, with the certainty of someone who had watched exactly four tutorial videos, that he would give her a box of handmade chocolates. Not bought ones. Ones he had tempered himself, so they came out glossy and broke with a clean snap, like the photograph in the video where the creator tapped a shard against the counter and it cracked like ice.

"You know you can buy chocolate at the store," Kolton said from the doorway, drying his hair with a towel. "Like, in a box. Already made."

"It's not the same thing," Alexander said, and then, because that sounded worse out loud than it had in his head, he added, "Tempering is the hard part. If I can do that, the rest is just pouring."

He chopped the bars into small, even pieces on the cutting board, reserving a third of them in a bowl on the side. The method he'd chosen was called seeding: melt most of the chocolate to about body temperature, then beat in the reserved chunks, which would cool the whole mass gradually and, if the video was right, coax the fat crystals into the one stable form out of the six that existed. Six forms, and only one of them behaved. He found that detail both reassuring and faintly ominous. It suggested that order was not the natural state of chocolate, that shininess was a kind of argument you had to win.

The bowl went over a pot of barely simmering water. He stirred with a spatula and watched the thermometer creep past ninety degrees, and Kolton leaned on the counter and told him about his older brother, who was contesting their grandfather's will on the grounds that primogeniture, the old rule of everything going to the eldest son, should not apply to a farming business that the younger brother had actually worked for eleven years. "He's not wrong," Kolton said. "But he's also doing it in a way that means nobody talks at Christmas."

Alexander said that was rough, and meant it, but his attention kept sliding back to the bowl, where the chocolate had gone fully liquid and dark and smelled like something he wanted to live inside. He lifted the bowl off the heat, wiped the bottom dry, and began adding the seed chocolate a handful at a time, stirring steadily, watching the temperature fall. Kolton got drafted into holding the thermometer and calling out numbers like a coxswain. Eighty-eight. Eighty-five. Eighty-two.

At eighty-one degrees, Alexander tested it by dipping the tip of a knife and setting it on the counter. In the video, the streak set in two minutes with a satin sheen. His stayed wet. At three minutes it was still tacky, and at five it had begun to firm with a dull, streaky surface, like a fingerprint pressed into old paint. He stood over it with the incipient panic of someone watching a plan die in slow motion. "I don't understand," he said. "I hit the temperature."

Kolton picked up one of the seed chunks Alexander hadn't used, turned it over, and read the label on the bag they'd come from. "Hey. Says here these are candy melts." He squinted. "It says coating chocolate. Compound, actually." He held it out. Alexander took the bag and read the ingredient list, which ran through a series of oils he did not recognize, and then, near the bottom, he saw it: palm kernel oil where he would have expected cocoa butter. He looked up compound chocolate on his phone with chocolate-smeared thumbs, and the first result told him that compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all cocoa butter with other fats, sets without tempering but does not have the same snap.

"So that's why my cousin just melts those and pours them at the campsite," Kolton said, peering over his shoulder. "She never tempers anything. I thought she was just lazy."

"It sets on its own," Alexander said slowly. "You don't have to temper it. But it doesn't snap the same." He turned back to the bowl of failed, streaky chocolate, and something in him let go of its grip on the plan and started thinking instead. He had two hours and one box of molds. If he wanted the real thing, glossy and brittle and difficult, he had no more bars of actual chocolate and no car, because his mother had taken it to work. If he wanted anything at all in a box tonight, it would be compound, easy and slightly waxy, honest about what it was.

He stood at the counter with the phone in one hand and the spatula in the other, weighing it. Maybe the difficulty was the point of the gift, a way of saying something he couldn't say at the party. Or maybe that was vanity, dressing up a candy box as a declaration, and the truest thing he could give her was the thing he could actually finish. He scraped the failed batch back into the bowl, set it over the warm pot, and began melting it down flat, to start again as itself. Kolton found a silicone mold shaped like fish in the pantry. "She likes fish," Kolton said. "She told me once."

"They're terrible," Alexander said, pouring. The compound chocolate ran smooth and obedient into every scale and fin. Kolton set the timer for the freezer, and Alexander licked the spatula and handed it over so Kolton could too.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: A primary source was produced at the time being studied, such as a letter or diary, while a secondary source, such as a textbook, interprets the past later using primary sources.
story:
The museum's basement archive smelled of paper that had survived longer than anyone who wrote it. Thomas had taken the volunteer job because Mr. Flores needed a body for the summer and because his mother said a résumé line never hurt. He had not expected to spend July in a room with no windows, a humming dehumidifier, and a metal cart of documents someone's granddaughter had donated in a cardboard box tied with butcher's twine.

"They were my grandmother's," the granddaughter had told Mr. Flores at the front desk that morning, before Thomas carried the box downstairs. "From when she was a nurse in the war. Nobody in the family wants them, but nobody wanted to burn them either." Mr. Flores had signed a form and thanked her, and now the box sat under a lamp waiting to be sorted, which was apparently Thomas's job, because Merrick had called in sick and Mr. Flores was upstairs arguing with a consultant about the new exhibit labels.

Ivy arrived at noon, ostensibly to bring Thomas a sandwich, actually because she was bored. She cut the twine with her keys and lifted out a bundle of letters, and the way she held them, careful, almost formal, made Thomas slow down. The envelopes were thin, the ink faded to a brownish color, and the stamps had a face on them he recognized from a textbook chapter he had half forgotten.

"These are the real thing," Ivy said, reading over his shoulder. "Not a textbook telling you about it later. It's like when we did that unit in Mr. Flores's class." She tapped an envelope. "A primary source, one produced at the time, a letter or a diary. A textbook is a secondary source. It interprets the past afterward, using these."

"I know," Thomas said, though he had mostly known it as a definition to be memorized, a line on a study sheet, and here it was a smell of old glue and a nurse's slanted handwriting apologizing for a tear in the paper where she said she had cried on it.

They read for two hours. The nurse, whose name was Dora, wrote to a sister about ward conditions, about a doctor she did not trust, about a young man from Ohio who had died on a Tuesday. In one letter she described an incident at the hospital, a shortage that had gone badly, and she wrote around it, saying only that those who were there knew what happened and she would not put it in a letter. Thomas read it twice and felt the strange weight of a fact being deliberately withheld, a hole shaped exactly like something.

Upstairs, later, he found Mr. Flores in the gallery where the labels were being replaced. Thomas asked whether the new exhibit would mention the hospital shortage. Mr. Flores laughed, not unkindly. "Which version? I've read three accounts of that. A doctor's memoir, an official report, and now, apparently, a nurse's letters that decline to confirm any of them. Historians have been arguing about it for decades. Some fellow published a revisionist take a few years back, claimed the whole story had been embellished, and half the field wanted him drawn and quartered." He looked at the label copy on his desk, a single sentence about the war's home front, and seemed to be trying to resuscitate it into something that could hold a disagreement. "Every source is partial, Thomas. Written by someone, for someone, with something left out. And every generation asks new questions of the old sources, so the answers keep moving."

Thomas thought about the definition he had memorized in the spring, how flat it had seemed, and how different it felt now, holding the partial thing itself. He had assumed the archive was where the past got settled, and instead it seemed to be where it stayed open.

That evening, back in the basement, Ivy had gone home and the dehumidifier droned like something lugubrious and patient. Thomas laid out three documents on the table: Dora's letter that said nothing directly, the official report Mr. Flores had photocopied for him, and a page from a textbook he'd found in the reference shelf that summarized the incident in four confident sentences. He looked at them side by side and could not make them agree. The report gave one number of patients. The textbook, written later, gave the same number but a different cause. Dora's letter gave no number, only a Tuesday and a torn page.

He sat with all three for a long moment. Then he pulled his notebook over and wrote, at the top of a fresh page, "What actually happened, and who gets to say." Under it he made three columns, one for each source, and left the bottom of the page blank.

"You coming up?" Mr. Flores called from the stairs. "We lock at six."

"In a minute," Thomas said, and wrote Dora's name in the margin.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Supercompensation is the idea that the body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself.
story:
Ryder climbed the lifeguard ladder at six in the morning because the pool was empty then, and empty meant no one could count his laps. He had been coming every day for eleven days, sometimes twice, and he kept his splits folded in the pocket of his shorts like a confession he wasn't ready to make. The clock on the far wall ticked through its flip numbers, obsolescent as everything else in this town, and he pushed off before it reached the minute.

The plan had seemed simple when he'd made it. The county championships were in five weeks, and the kid from Riverside had beaten him by four tenths of a second last season, which was less than a breath, less than a hesitation at the turn. So Ryder had done the arithmetic the way he did everything, bluntly: more yards, more mornings, more of everything until the gap closed. He had written the program on the back of his chemistry notes, Monday through Sunday with no blank squares, because blank squares felt like surrender.

On Tuesday he swam the hundred in a time he hadn't recorded since he was fourteen. He stood in the shallow end with his hands on his knees, watching the flip numbers settle, and told himself the clock was wrong. On Thursday he was slower again. He checked the clock against his phone, and his phone against the microwave in the staff room, and both agreed, and something in his chest went quiet and cold.

"You look like a guy exhuming his own race," Ali said from the deck on Friday, towel around her neck. She had watched him squinting at the splits on his crumpled paper, smoothing it flat against the concrete. Ali was the one who read everything, who could explain the phonetics of Ryder's weird vowel-laden last name at a party once, tracing it back through two languages until everyone was bored except him. He folded the paper and said it was nothing.

But on Saturday, when he climbed the ladder and Dimitri was already there, uncoiling the lane ropes, the nothing became too heavy to carry alone. Dimitri had been swimming year-round since they were ten, and he had a way of listening with his whole body, arms still, head tilted. Ryder told him everything: the eleven days, the double sessions, the times going the wrong direction, the paper in his pocket. Then he pulled it out and handed it over, and watched Dimitri read it, waiting for the verdict with the same dread he'd waited for the clock.

"Every day," Dimitri said.

"I'm getting slower," Ryder said. "I don't understand it. I'm working harder than I ever have."

Dimitri set the paper down on the deck and tapped one blank corner of it. "My club coach calls it supercompensation," he said. "The body gets fitter during recovery, not during the workout. That's when it rebuilds, past where it was before." He tapped again, the empty square where Sunday should have been. "You've been giving it nothing to rebuild with."

Ryder sat down on the edge of the gutter, feet in the water, and looked at the program he had built so carefully. It was a good plan in every way except the one that mattered, a machine with no off switch, and he understood now that the blank squares he'd hated were not surrender but the actual engine of the thing. Maybe. He turned it over in his mind, the way Ali turned over words, and he could not fully make the two ideas fit: that effort created the possibility of speed and also withheld it. He knew only that the clock had voted, and the clock did not care about his arithmetic.

"So what do I do," he said, "just stop?"

"Not stop. Rest. Warm up slow, work hard, then take the day off like it's part of the training." Dimitri handed the paper back. "Write it in. Ink, so you can't cheat."

Ryder asked the front desk for a pen, and on the concrete, in the flat morning light, he drew squares into Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, and wrote one word in each one, small enough that it looked almost like a lane line.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: In Chicago, MLA and APA styles, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited.
story:
The librarian at the front desk had told Taylor the study room was reserved for the writing club until five, and Taylor had said she was in the writing club, which was true in the sense that she had come to the meeting twice and intended to keep coming until Mr. Ahmadi stopped noticing that she never paid the two-dollar dues. She spread her materials across the table: eleven sources photocopied from the reference section, a stack of index cards, and the paper itself, seven pages about municipal water fluoridation, due Thursday. She had finished the footnotes the night before. All that remained was the bibliography, which she assumed was a formality, and she numbered the entries in the order she had cited them, starting with the county health department report because it had come first in the paper.

Zachery arrived at four with a frozen coffee that dripped onto the table every time he set it down. He was the only other member who had come that day, and he leaned over her pages without asking, the way he did with everything. "What's this list at the end?" he said.

"The bibliography. Chicago style, because that's what Mr. Ahmadi assigned." She tapped the pages square. "Eleven sources. I only needed eight, so I'm already ahead."

"You put them in the order you cited them."

"Obviously. That's how I used them."

He pulled the style guide off the shelf behind him, the thick orange one with the cracked spine that lived in the study room, and turned to a page near the back. Then he slid it across the table, open, his finger on a paragraph. "In Chicago, MLA and APA styles, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited."

Taylor read the paragraph twice. "That makes no sense. The whole point of an order is to show the sequence."

"It's not a sequence. It's so people can find things." He wiped his cup ring with his sleeve. "Nobody's scanning your footnotes and then hunting through a random list."

She wanted to argue further, and she had a good argument loaded, something about the reader's experience of the paper as a progressive document, but she also noticed that her desire to argue had begun to enervate her, the way defending a position she half-knew was wrong always did, a slow draining that started behind the eyes. She picked up a pencil instead.

The recopying took forty minutes. She alphabetized by surname, which required discovering that the county health department report had no author at all and had to be filed under the agency name, and that the article by K. R. Aden came before the book by Aden and Whitfield, or after, and the guide was unclear enough about that single-author-versus-two-author question that she had to make a judgment call and mark it with a small asterisk to ask Mr. Ahmadi. When she finished, the list looked strange to her, wrong in a way she couldn't articulate, like a song with the verses shuffled. She said so.

"That's because you wrote the paper as a story," Zachery said. "You had this leitmotif, this thing about trust, coming back in every section. The sources in citation order reinforced it. Alphabetical breaks that."

"Then alphabetical is worse."

"Or the argument should be strong enough to survive the shuffle." He said it mildly and went back to his own laptop, where he was writing something about wetland restoration, footnotes already alphabetized, she couldn't help noticing.

Taylor sat with both versions for a while, the citation-order draft on her left, the alphabetical on her right. She thought about Mr. Ahmadi, who had said on the first day that a research paper was not a report but an argument, that the reader should be able to disagree with it. And she thought about what Zachery had said, that the rules existed for readers she would never meet, readers who wanted to check her claims rather than follow her arc. Those were two different pictures of the same document: one hers, shaped and intentional, and one that belonged to a system that didn't care about her intentions at all. She had spent most of high school assuming the second picture was just bureaucracy, but sitting between the two lists, she could see that a reader checking a claim in footnote fourteen didn't want to relive her discovery process. That reader wanted the name and the page. Maybe order and findability weren't opposites; maybe the footnotes carried the sequence and the bibliography carried the map, and the paper needed both because readers needed both.

She was aware that this was the kind of reasoning she performed for teachers, the neat synthesis, and she didn't fully trust it. She still felt the loss of the citation order, which had been, she admitted only inwardly, a small vanity, a way of making the research read like a quest with her at the center. Whether alphabetical was truly better for a reader or just convention hardened into requirement, she couldn't decide, and she suspected Mr. Ahmadi would say the distinction didn't matter. She wrote the asterisk question in the margin anyway: How do I cite a source with no author? Then, beneath it, a second question she did not plan to ask aloud: Does the order of the list change what counts as evidence?

At five to five she began packing. Zachery stacked the photocopied sources for her, out of his habit of arranging other people's things, and the pages made a small evolution in his hands, the Aden article sliding from the top to somewhere in the middle, alphabetical even in the pile.

"Mr. Ahmadi's going to think you did this all along," he said.

"He's going to think I read the guide."

"You did read the guide."

"After you opened it for me." She took the pile from him and squared it against the table edge. Outside, the October light had gone thin and evanescent over the parking lot, already half gone behind the bank across the street. She zipped her bag and said, "Same time next week. I'm paying the dues."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Programmers describe linear search as O(n), meaning its work grows in step with the list, and binary search as O(log n), meaning its work grows with the logarithm of the list's size.
story:
The whiteboard in the lodge still held yesterday's tournament bracket when Coralie came down for breakfast, and beneath it, in her own handwriting from a late and half-remembered fit of note taking, the phrase "O(log n)". She had written it after lights out, when Ms. Ba's evening talk about algorithms was still circling in her head, and now, in the grey morning light coming off the riparian trail, it looked like an accusation. In forty minutes the whole group would vote on which search method to build into their camp project: a lookup table for the canoe inventory, five hundred sorted entries, and two ways to find one.

Marko slid into the seat across from her with his tray. "You're staring at the board like it owes you money."

"I know what it means," Coralie said. "I just don't know if I can say it out loud without mangling it."

"You wrote it."

"That's different. Writing is private. Talking is a performance in front of the polity." She gestured at the dining hall, where the other campers were shovelling eggs and arguing about the previous night's capture-the-flag rulings.

Ms. Ba had set the terms the night before: anyone could advocate for a method, then the group would vote, and the winning implementation had to be explained by its advocate to the visiting programmer on Friday. Coralie wanted that job. She had wanted it since Monday, when she'd spent an hour watching a linear search crawl through a list of names and felt, physically, the drag of it, one entry at a time, like reading a phone book with your thumb. But wanting something and being able to argue for it were, she was beginning to suspect, different skills entirely.

After breakfast the group reconvened in the lodge. Angel went first, championing the linear search on the grounds that anyone could understand it. "You check each item until you find the one you want," Angel said, tapping the table. "Simple. Honest. No tricks." A few people nodded.

Then Ms. Ba looked at the whiteboard, at the scrawled phrase, and then at Coralie. "That's yours, I think. Before we vote, can you tell the group what it says and why it matters?"

Coralie stood. Her chair scraped. She had meant to ruminate on the walk over, to arrange her sentences, but Angel had wanted to stop at the dock to watch a heron, and there had gone her thinking time. So she began with the heron, oddly, because it was in her head. "Imagine the list is the lake," she said. "The linear search wades along the whole shoreline to find one thing. The binary search doesn't. The list is sorted, so every time you look at the middle, you learn which half your item is in, and you get to ignore the other half entirely. You keep halving."

"Okay," said Angel, arms crossed but listening.

"So the work doesn't grow the same way for the two methods. Programmers describe linear search as O(n), meaning its work grows in step with the list. If the list gets ten times longer, the search gets roughly ten times slower. And they describe binary search as O(log n), meaning its work grows with the logarithm of the list's size. The list can grow enormously and the search only creeps up. That's what I wrote on the board. That's the whole argument."

"Prove it," Marko said, not unkindly. "Not the notation. The halving."

So they did it as a scene, right there. Ms. Ba held up the printed inventory, and Angel picked a canoe serial number from a scrap of paper and refused to show it. Coralie opened the binder at the middle page, read the serial there, and said, "Yours comes after this, so I only need the back half." She halved it again. Again. On the eighth look she found the number, and Angel turned the scrap of paper around to confirm, looking faintly betrayed by her own success.

"Eight," Angel said. "Out of five hundred."

"Roughly eight," Coralie said. "A linear search might have needed the whole five hundred, depending on where it hid." She hesitated, because honesty was the part she'd decided not to skip. "It's slower to code and it only works because the list is sorted, so if the inventory stops being sorted, it breaks silently. That's the cost. I still think it's worth it, but that's the trade, and I'd rather we vote knowing it."

Ms. Ba raised her hand. "All in favour of binary search."

Coralie counted the hands and lost track somewhere past eleven, and Marko was grinning at her, and outside the heron lifted off the dock, slow and low across the water.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: François Furet's 1978 book, translated as Interpreting the French Revolution, argued the French should stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history.
story:
Abigail had promised herself she would start the historiography essay on Saturday, and it was now Thursday, and all she had produced was a document titled "FRENCH REV THING" containing the sentence "Historians have disagreed," followed by a page break and the courage of the truly stalled. The assignment from Mr. Greco was short and terrible: trace how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800, and take a position of your own. Nine hundred words of other people's arguments, and then, at the end, her own name attached to an opinion. She had opinions about plenty of things, such as whether the cafeteria's turkey club was legally a sandwich, but she had never before been asked to hold one about two hundred years of scholarship.

She went to the library after last period, partly to work and partly because Jenna had texted her a photo of a carton of blueberry muffins with the caption "third floor, come defend your sandwich thesis." Trinity was already there, laying out the muffins like a general reviewing troops. Abigail spread her notes across the table: the classical view of the Revolution as the dawn of modern liberty, then the Marxists who saw class war, then something in the 1970s where, as far as she could tell, everyone simply stopped agreeing, the debate turning turbid and loud, like a river after a storm, and just as hard to see the bottom of.

"You look like the muffins insulted you," Trinity said.

"The books insult me. Half of them say 1789 changed everything, half say it changed nothing, and they all hate each other in French." Abigail flipped through her list of sources, which Mr. Greco had annotated with a cheerful "dig deeper!" that she took as a threat. "And then there's this one, a 1978 book by a guy named Furet, and I can't even tell whose side it's on."

Jenna, who was highlighting her chemistry notes in a color scheme that suggested traffic lights, peered over. "Furet. Like the ferret."

"It is not like the ferret."

"It is absolutely like the ferret."

The library owned one copy of the translated book, shelved in a section so far back it felt like a border crossing, the isthmus of the stacks connecting nonfiction to the forgotten. Abigail found it wedged between two thicker volumes, its spine faded to the color of weak tea. She carried it back to the table, ate a muffin out of pure nerves, and started skimming the introduction, which was dense in the way that made her suspect the author of being right about something.

"Wait," she said, twenty minutes later, out loud, before she could stop herself.

"She speaks," said Trinity.

"Okay, so. The Marxists basically said the Revolution was class conflict, and after that you had to read everything through it. And this Furet guy, in 1978, the book got translated as Interpreting the French Revolution. And his whole argument, or a big part of it, is that the French should stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history. Like, everyone had made 1789 the hinge everything else swings on, and he's saying, take it off the hinge."

Jenna frowned. "Isn't that like arguing the Revolution didn't matter?"

"No, it's sneakier than that. It matters, it's just not the master key. Like, imagine if the only thing anyone ever asked about your whole life was the summer you turned fourteen."

"That was a bad summer," Jenna said. "I got braces and a mullet."

"See, and the mullet was real, but it doesn't explain your grades or your taste in men. Historians had been explaining all of France by the mullet of 1789."

Trinity laughed loud enough that the librarian looked over with the mild, permanent disappointment of her office. "That's going in the essay. The mullet of 1789."

"It is not going in the essay." But Abigail was already writing, fast, in the margin of her draft, and what she was writing was not a summary of either side. Because she had liked the Marxist account too, honestly; there was something in the idea of a class throwing off its chains that had made her feel, reading it on the bus, like history could emancipate people, or at least describe how they had emancipated themselves. Furet did not exactly disprove that. He narrowed it. He took a story that had explained everything and made it explain less, and the strange thing was that it seemed to her more trustworthy afterward, not less, the way a friend who admits uncertainty is more believable than one who never does.

Her problem, then, was not that she had no position. Her problem was that her position was a both. The older view still held something true about why the Revolution seized people's imaginations; the 1978 turn held something true about the cost of letting one event explain a whole country. Her position had a hinge problem of its own, and she worked on the last paragraph until the lights overhead buzzed and the librarian began her closing circuit, and she wrote the final sentence with the clock against her, and did not entirely love it, and handed it in anyway.

Mr. Greco returned the essays a week later. He had written "dig deeper!" again at the bottom, which she chose to read as an invitation rather than a verdict, and beside her both/and paragraph he had drawn a small crooked star. She carried it to the third floor, where Trinity examined the star with clinical suspicion.

"Is a star good?"

"It's a star," Abigail said. "I'm taking the star."

story:
The licensing office smelled of hand sanitizer and burnt coffee, and Connor stood in line behind a girl who kept rereading the same poster while her number crawled closer to being called. He had been half watching her, half watching his own hands on the laminated permit form, when the poster's headline finally snagged his attention. It was a CDC statistic, printed in the kind of blue that licensing offices apparently believed was calming: drivers aged 16 to 19 had a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven. He read it twice. Almost three times. Per mile, which meant it wasn't just that teenagers drove more or drove less; it was the mileage itself that was dangerous when the driver was his age.

"Excuse me," the girl said, turning around suddenly, as if she had felt him reading over her shoulder. She had a textbook under one arm, chemistry by the look of the diagrams. "Does that number seem right to you? Almost three times. I'm Lyna, by the way."

"Connor." He looked at the poster again, transfixed by the smallness of the claim, its refusal to explain itself. "It doesn't say why. It just says the rate."

"That's what's bothering me," Lyna said. "They put it up like it's supposed to make me a better driver, but it doesn't tell me anything I can do about it. Except not drive. Which is the opposite of why I'm here."

Reese appeared beside them with two vending machine cookies and an expression that Connor had once described in a group chat as saturnine, and Reese had replied that he wasn't gloomy, he was realistic, which everyone agreed was the same thing. "You're staring at a poster," Reese said. "On purpose. Before your first lesson."

"It says we're almost three times as likely to die," Connor said.

"Per mile," Reese said, because he had apparently read it too, on his own trip here last month, when he had passed his permit test and then failed to book a single lesson out of what he called laziness and everyone else called fear. "Which my dad says is a rigged comparison, because old people drive more highway miles, and highway miles are safer, so it evens out." He tore the cookie wrapper with his teeth. "Anyway, statistically you're fine. Statistically, we're all fine."

"That's not what statistically means," Lyna said.

"It's exactly what statistically means. Most teenagers don't die. Therefore, fine."

The argument might have gone on, except that a voice from the counter called C-47, and Connor's stomach performed a small rearrangement. That was him. He stepped forward, handed over his form, had his vision checked through a machine that smelled like a dentist's office, and was told to report to the driving school van in the lot behind the building, where an instructor was waiting. The instructor was Mr. Banerjee, who had a clipboard, a second set of pedals bolted into the passenger side, and a manner that suggested he had seen every possible way a first lesson could go wrong and had decided in advance not to take any of it personally.

"Seatbelt," Mr. Banerjee said. "Mirror. Seat. We begin in the lot, then the neighborhood streets, then, if you are not a catastrophe, the main road."

Connor's hands were on the wheel before he realized he hadn't decided whether he wanted to be here. That was the thing he had been circling all morning, the thing the poster had sharpened into a point. He had signed up because Reese had signed up, because everyone signed up, because turning eighteen without a license was starting to feel like arriving at a pool party without a swimsuit. But the number on the poster was real, and no one had disputed it, and his mother's voice was in his head saying drive safe in the tone she used for things she thought he wouldn't do. He wanted the independence. He also wanted, with a sincerity he found slightly embarrassing, to not be a statistic.

"Should I be more careful than I think I need to be?" he asked Mr. Banerjee, easing the van forward in first gear, then second, the clutch shuddering under his foot. "There was a poster in there. About the crash rate for people my age."

Mr. Banerjee did not launch into speech, which Connor appreciated. He adjusted the mirror on his side and said only, "What did the poster say?"

"That drivers my age have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers twenty and older. Per mile driven."

"Then you know more than most of my students. Turn left at the cone."

Connor turned left, too widely, corrected, and thought about Reese in the waiting room, probably telling Lyna that the risk was an average and averages were for other people. And it was true that the statistic was an average, that it folded every reckless teenager and every careful one into a single number, that it could not tell him which kind he was. That was the honest uncertainty at the center of the whole morning. He could not know, in advance, whether he was the kind of driver the number was describing. The only thing he could control was how he drove, which was a small answer to a large question, and he drove the next three blocks like a man trying to make the answer true.

Afterward, back in the lot, the van parked and the engine ticking, Connor found Reese sitting on the curb with Lyna, both of them holding the paper permits that had cost an hour of multiple choice. "How was it?" Reese asked, and there was something underneath the question, something Connor recognized because he had heard it in his own voice for weeks.

"I was scared the whole time," Connor said. "I went anyway. That's basically the whole story." He held out his hand. "You want to book your lesson now? I'll sit in the back."

Reese looked at the van, then at the curb, then at his phone, and pulled up the driving school's number. "Tuesday," he said to Lyna, or to himself. "I'm doing it Tuesday."

"Put it on speaker," Lyna said. "I want to hear a human being confirm this actually happened."
